text: Two vast hospital-asylums on the southern edge of Paris. The Salpêtrière, built on an old gunpowder (saltpetre) works, held poor, mad and 'fallen' women; Bicêtre, just outside the wall, was its male counterpart and also a prison. Hugo places the Gorbeau house between them, 'between the madness of women and the madness of men'.
quote: between the Salpêtrière, a glimpse of whose dome could be seen, and Bicêtre

text: One of the toll gates in the wall of the Farmers-General, the customs wall that still ringed Paris in 1823. Goods entering the city paid duty there, so the barriers were cheap, rough districts of wine-shops and waste ground. The Barrière d'Italie and the Barrière Saint-Jacques are on the road out to Bicêtre; the latter became the site of public executions.
quote: In 1823 the city wall was still in existence.

text: The square in front of the Paris town hall where public executions had been carried out for centuries. Hugo calls the gallows set up by the elms of the Barrière Saint-Jacques a 'shop-keeping and bourgeois' Grève: a society that would neither abolish the death penalty nor own it openly moved the scaffold out of sight.
quote: that miserable and shameful Place de Grève of a shop-keeping and bourgeois society

text: The old fortress on the right bank that housed the chief law courts and a prison of royal Paris; it was demolished early in the century. The attorneys Corbeau and Renard who gave the house its name practised there about 1770.
quote: two attorneys at the Châtelet named, one Corbeau (Raven), the other Renard (Fox)

text: The opening of La Fontaine's fable 'The Crow and the Fox', in which a flattering fox talks a crow out of its cheese: every French schoolchild knew it by heart. The courthouse wags replaced the tree with a legal file and the cheese with a writ of seizure, and the two lawyers petitioned the king to change their names.
quote: Maître Corbeau, sur un dossier perché

text: The last mistress of Louis XV, a former shop-girl raised to the court in 1769. Hugo's anecdote of a papal nuncio and a cardinal putting slippers on her bare feet is a jab at the servility of the old regime's clergy, slipped in while explaining a house name.
quote: putting on, in his Majesty’s presence, a slipper on the bare feet of Madame du Barry

text: The Paris–Orléans line, whose terminus (today the Gare d'Austerlitz) opened in 1840 beside the Salpêtrière. Hugo, writing in the 1860s, keeps stepping out of 1823 to say what has become of these places since; the railway is his emblem of the suburb being swallowed by the city.
quote: a railway station is the death of a suburb and the birth of a city

text: The poor working quarter of the left bank around the Rue Mouffetard and the Bièvre tanneries, long a byword for misery. Hugo's 'suburb of Saint-Marceau' is where paved streets only arrived, he says, in July 1845.
quote: Paris had entered the suburb of Saint-Marceau

text: Hapgood's rendering of the French cabinet: a small closet-room off a main chamber, big enough for a folding bed. Cheap Paris lodgings were described by their rooms and cabinets; a cabinet alone, without a fireplace, could be let as a dwelling.
quote: At the extreme end there was a dressing-room with a folding bed

text: Loans floated by the Spanish liberal government of 1820–23 and repudiated after the French army restored King Ferdinand VII in 1823, ruining many French holders. 'A gentleman ruined by Spanish bonds' was therefore a plausible story in December 1823, and an excuse for living poorly on hidden money.
quote: a gentleman of means who had been ruined by Spanish bonds

text: In a Paris house the principale locataire rented the whole building from the owner and sublet the rooms, usually serving as portress and cleaner as well. Hugo mocks the grand title; she is the only neighbour and the only eyes in the Gorbeau house.
quote: ornamented with the name of the “principal lodger,” and in reality entrusted with the functions of portress

text: Red, cracked, itching swellings on the hands and feet caused by repeated exposure to cold: the mark of a child who has worked outdoors and slept unheated. Cosette's hands still carry Montfermeil.
quote: her tiny red hand, all cracked with chilblains

text: Black clothes worn for a dead relative; even small children were dressed in black. The 'little black gown' Valjean bought at Montfermeil is mourning for Fantine, though Cosette does not know who she is mourning.
quote: Cosette was no longer in rags; she was in mourning.

text: The parish church of the Faubourg Saint-Marceau, at the foot of the Rue Mouffetard, a few minutes from the Gorbeau house. Its churchyard was notorious in the 1730s for the 'convulsionaries', Jansenist devotees who fell into fits at a deacon's tomb, a story Hugo alludes to elsewhere.
quote: He liked to go to Saint-Médard, which is the nearest church.

text: The Bank of France printed notes in large denominations only; a thousand-franc note was a year's wages for a labourer and something a poor woman might see two or three times in her life. Sewn into the lining of a shabby coat it is the stuff of neighbourhood legend.
quote: a bank-bill for a thousand francs. It was the second or third only that she had seen

text: The nickname the Faubourg Saint-Marceau gives the shabby old man who accepts a sou from kind women and slips silver to beggars when he thinks no one is looking. Valjean's disguise works too well: a contradiction gets talked about.
quote: under the name of “the beggar who gives alms.”

text: A lay church officer (the French suisse) who kept order during services, carrying a staff and wearing a cocked hat. An ex-beadle mumbling prayers by a church is a natural fixture; Hugo also lets us hear that some say he 'belongs to the police'.
quote: He was an ex-beadle of seventy-five

text: The large silver five-franc coin, still counted in sous by most people (the chapter title calls it a five-franc piece). Valjean is making up a roll of a hundred francs in these coins when one escapes and rings on the floor, a sound a listening house can hear.
quote: a hundred-sou piece escaped from his hands and rolled noisily on the floor

text: Hugo had been in exile since Louis-Napoléon's coup of December 1851, writing on Guernsey while Haussmann rebuilt Paris. This aside explains why he describes the city of his youth in the present tense and warns the reader that the streets he names may no longer exist.
quote: has been absent from Paris for many years

text: The art and vocabulary of the hunt. Hugo narrates the whole night pursuit in hunting terms: the stag doubling back on its track (which he calls 'false re-imbushment'), the hounds, the scent, the 'knowing dog'. Valjean is the hunted animal, Javert the huntsman.
quote: In venery this is called “false re-imbushment.”

text: The maze of old streets around the Rue Mouffetard on the left bank, between the Gorbeau house and the Panthéon. Hugo lists its lanes (Censier, Copeau, Puits-l'Ermite) like a map; Saint-Étienne-du-Mont, whose clock strikes eleven, is the church beside the Panthéon.
quote: many and varied labyrinths in the Mouffetard quarter

text: The commissaire de police, the salaried official in charge of a Paris district's police post, under the Prefect of Police. The lantern over his office in the Rue de Pontoise is what betrays the men following Valjean.
quote: in front of the office of the commissary of police, situated at No. 14

text: An iron bridge across the Seine by the Jardin des Plantes, finished in 1807 and named for Napoleon's victory. Like other new bridges it was built by a company that charged a toll, a sou a head, for decades; a man carrying a child who can walk pays for two.
quote: Tolls were still collected there at that epoch.

text: A real pottery in the Rue de la Clef whose rhymed sign Hugo quotes: 'Here is the factory of Goblet the son; come choose jugs and pitchers, flower-pots, pipes and brick; to all comers the Heart sells Diamonds (tiles).' The last line is a pun on playing-card suits and roof tiles.
quote: A tout venant le Coeur vend des Carreaux

text: The royal botanical garden and natural-history museum on the left bank near the river, with a small zoo. Valjean skirts it by the lower streets to reach the quay and the bridge.
quote: skirted the Jardin des Plantes by the lower streets, and reached the quay

text: Hugo's name for a half-built district of walls, gardens and convents between the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and the river port of La Râpée, so obscure that, he says, no existing map shows it and only the 1727 plan of Denis Thierry does. Its Y of streets (Chemin-Vert, Petit-Picpus, Polonceau) joined by the Rue Droit-Mur and ending in the blind alley Genrot is the trap Valjean has walked into.
quote: Le Petit-Picpus, which, moreover, hardly ever had any existence

text: A great cellular prison built in the 1840s near what is now the Gare de Lyon, on the ground Hugo is describing. He lists it among the 'improvements' of the new quarter as progress 'with its antidote'.
quote: railway stations, and a prison, Mazas, there

text: Examples of Paris's habit of keeping old names: the Collège des Quatre-Nations was the building that became the Institut de France, and the Opéra-Comique had played in the Rue Feydeau. Hugo lists such survivals (Porte Saint-Jacques, la Bourbe, la Petite-Pologne) as the people's memory of a vanished city.
quote: persists in calling the Institut les Quatre-Nations, and the Opera-Comique Feydeau

text: A fruit tree trained flat against a wall on a frame of branches. The old lead water-pipes branching across the convent façade look to Valjean like a leafless espalier, and for a moment like a ladder.
quote: This odd espalier, with its branches of lead and iron

text: The Conciergerie is the medieval prison on the Île de la Cité where the condemned waited for the scaffold. Battemolle, a man under sentence of death, is said to have escaped by climbing a corner of its wall by sheer muscle; Hugo cites him to show that Valjean's feat has precedents.
quote: that corner of the wall of the Conciergerie of Paris by which Battemolle, condemned to death, made his escape

text: Before gas (which came to Paris streets from the late 1820s), oil lanterns hung over the roadway from a rope stretched between walls and were lowered and raised with a pulley; the lamplighter kept the key to the little box that locked the rope. Not lit on moonlit nights, such a lantern is simply a rope waiting to be cut.
quote: they were ascended and descended by means of a rope, which traversed the street from side to side

term: 'Would have given it for a rope'
text: An echo of Shakespeare's Richard III crying 'My kingdom for a horse!' on Bosworth field. Hugo turns the king's cry into a convict's: the one thing he lacks at midnight is a rope.
quote: if Jean Valjean had had a kingdom, he would have given it for a rope at that moment

text: A sailor's knot (the French noeud d'hirondelle) that can be tied fast in a moment and will not slip. Valjean, who learned such things in the port of Toulon, uses it to fasten his cravat round Cosette to the lantern rope.
quote: which seafaring men call a “swallow knot,”

text: A long strip of linen or silk wound round the neck and knotted, worn by every man who was not in rags; a coat without a cravat looked half-dressed. Valjean's cravat becomes a harness, which is why Fauchelevent is shocked to find him without one.
quote: he undid his cravat, passed it round Cosette’s body under the armpits

term: 'Deaf stones of which the Scriptures speak'
text: The Bible repeatedly mocks idols of wood and stone that cannot hear or speak (Habakkuk 2:18–19, Psalm 115). Hugo borrows the image for the convent walls, which seem not to hear the uproar of the search outside them.
quote: those walls had been built of the deaf stones of which the Scriptures speak

text: The cloth in which a corpse is wrapped for burial: a shroud. Hugo's first glimpse into the convent is deliberately a vision of the grave, a form lying face down under what looks like a shroud, with a rope round its neck.
quote: something which appeared to be covered with a winding-sheet, and which resembled a human form

text: Glass domes (cloches) set over young melons and other tender plants to protect them from frost. Spreading straw mats over the melon bed on a bright, freezing night is exactly what a gardener would be doing at two in the morning.
quote: walking amid the bell-glasses of the melon beds

text: A bell buckled to the gardener's knee so that the nuns hear him coming and keep away; in a house of women no other man may enter but the archbishop. The 'tinkling like cattle bells' Valjean heard in the garden was this. Fauchelevent wears it with a wink.
quote: a leather kneecap, whence hung a moderately large bell

text: Mild rustic oaths, 'by God' with the blasphemy softened by mispronunciation, like 'parbleu' and 'morbleu'. Fauchelevent's speech is full of them; he is a peasant who was once a notary, and Hugo gives him a countryman's voluble tongue.
quote: “Ah! pardieu, this is too much!”

text: The headquarters of the Paris police, under a prefect appointed by the government; the Comte Anglès was prefect from 1815 to 1821, and M. Chabouillet his secretary. Being 'attached to the police force of Paris' was a promotion for a provincial inspector like Javert.
quote: M. Chabouillet, secretary of the Prefecture under Comte Anglès

text: The Duc d'Angoulême, nephew of Louis XVIII, commanded the French army that invaded Spain in 1823 to restore King Ferdinand VII's absolute power, and returned in triumph that December. A royalist like Javert would read a newspaper for this and nothing else.
quote: the triumphal entry of the Prince Generalissimo into Bayonne

text: The département that surrounded Paris on all sides, including Montfermeil; its prefecture was at Versailles. A report of a child stolen there would be forwarded to the Paris police as a matter of routine.
quote: a police report was transmitted from the prefecture of the Seine-et-Oise

term: The free press and the Chambers
text: In the early 1820s newspapers could still denounce police abuses, and deputies could raise them in the two Chambers (Deputies and Peers) of the constitutional monarchy. Hugo explains Javert's hesitation partly by this: an arrest of a respectable white-haired 'grandfather' that turned out wrong would be in twenty papers and cost the agent his place.
quote: the free press embarrassed it; several arbitrary arrests denounced by the newspapers

text: The look of a returned exile of the Revolution reduced to earning his bread as a tutor: shabby, genteel, elderly, harmless. Valjean's yellow coat and careful manners read that way to Javert, and the altered gait of a man pacing himself to a child's steps completes the picture.
quote: his costume of an émigré-preceptor

term: Attila, Hannibal at Capua, Danton at Arcis
text: Three famous hesitations: Attila wavering between the eastern and western Roman emperors, Hannibal idling at Capua instead of marching on Rome, Danton lingering at his home at Arcis-sur-Aube in 1794 while his enemies prepared his arrest. Hugo ranks Javert's lost quarter-hour at the Carrefour Rollin with them.
quote: it is Hannibal tarrying at Capua; it is Danton falling asleep at Arcis-sur-Aube

text: Old authorities on stag-hunting whom Hugo cites as if they were generals. When a stag escapes with the pack at its heels, the hunters, he says, are left saying 'it was not a stag, but a sorcerer'.
quote: Duvivier, Ligniville, and Desprez halt short.

text: The magic words that open the robbers' cave in 'Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves' from the Arabian Nights. Getting past the convent's porter, and then past the voice behind the grating, needs passwords that only the initiated know.
quote: there was an Open Sesame! which it was necessary to know

term: Nankin paper at fifteen sous the roll
text: Cheap wallpaper in the buff colour of nankeen cotton, sold at three-quarters of a franc a roll. Hugo prices it to make the point: the visitors' room of this convent is as bare and poor as a servant's attic.
quote: hung with nankin paper with green flowers, at fifteen sous the roll

text: A ground-floor theatre box, so called because its shape recalls a bathtub, closed off from the house by a grille until the chandelier is lit. Hugo uses it to make the reader feel the convent parlour: a dark box facing a stage that stays shuttered.
quote: when one enters at the theatre into a grated baignoire

text: The wimple: the piece of linen or wool covering a nun's neck and breast up to the chin, here black. With the veil it leaves only the mouth and chin visible, which is all a visitor to this parlour ever sees of a nun.
quote: One caught a glimpse of a black guimpe

text: The one room of a closed convent where nuns may speak to outsiders, always through a grating; in strict houses a shutter behind the grating is opened only for close relatives. The Petit-Picpus version, with its double grille, perforated tin plate and black shutters, is the harshest Hugo knows.
quote: The box in which you stood was the parlor.

text: The order of the Petit-Picpus nuns as Hugo describes it: Benedictines following a Spanish reform he dates to 1425, dependent on Cîteaux and so 'Bernardine' in name, under the rule of Saint Benedict made harsher. Historians have not found Martin Verga; the real nuns of the Rue Picpus were Benedictines of the Blessed Sacrament, and Hugo seems to have combined and disguised his sources.
quote: a community of Bernardines of the obedience of Martin Verga

text: Benedict of Nursia (c. 480–547) wrote the rule that governs Western monks and founded Monte Cassino; Hugo repeats the legend of him driving the devil from a temple of Apollo at Subiaco. Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153) led the Cistercian reform of that rule. The chapter's tangle of orders (Cluny, Cîteaux, Carthusians and the rest) all descend from Benedict.
quote: they were the subjects, not of Saint Bernard, but of Saint Benoît

text: An order of nuns reformed by Teresa of Ávila in the 1560s, famous for its severity: barefoot (hence 'Discalced'), fasting, silent. Hugo ranks only their rule above that of the Petit-Picpus.
quote: After the rule of the Carmelites, who go barefoot

text: The devotion of keeping at least one nun kneeling before the consecrated Host, day and night, without interruption, the sisters relieving one another hourly 'like soldiers on guard'. It gives the convent its name and sets its clock: the bell that interrupts everything on the hour, the twelve-hour 'reparation', the night office.
quote: there is always a sister kneeling before the Holy Sacrament … This is the Perpetual Adoration.

text: The Petit-Picpus practice by which one nun in turn kneels for twelve hours on the stone before the altar, a rope round her neck, praying for all the sins of the world, lying flat with arms outstretched when she can no longer kneel. Because it is done before a post holding a candle, the nuns say 'to be at the post', preferring the phrase that sounds like a punishment.
quote: with hands clasped, a rope around her neck

text: The mères vocales are the senior professed nuns who have a voice in the chapter, the governing assembly; they elect the prioress, who rules the house for a three-year term and may be re-elected twice. Below them come the professed sisters, lay-sisters who do manual work, novices and postulants.
quote: the mothers, who are called mères vocales because they have a voice in the chapter

text: Benedictine nuns of the Perpetual Adoration who had two Paris houses at the start of the century, at the Temple and in the Rue Neuve-Sainte-Geneviève, wearing a white wimple and a gilt emblem of the Host. Hugo insists they are not the Petit-Picpus order, though both practise the same devotion.
quote: the Benedictines called Ladies of the Holy Sacrament

term: The Oratory: Philip Neri and Bérulle
text: Two societies of priests of the same name: the Italian Oratory founded by Philip Neri in Rome in the 1560s and the French Oratory founded by Cardinal Pierre de Bérulle in 1611. Hugo's joke is that the French one claimed precedence because a cardinal outranks a saint.
quote: Philip de Neri was only a saint, while Bérulle was a cardinal

text: The breviary is the book of the daily round of psalms and prayers (the 'office') that religious are bound to recite; matins is its night portion. The Petit-Picpus nuns rise between one and three in the morning to chant it, which is why singing is heard from a dark convent at that hour.
quote: rise from their first sleep, from one to three o’clock in the morning, to read their breviary and chant matins

text: Coarse, scratchy woollen cloths. The nuns sleep between serge sheets and wear a drugget shift against the skin from 14 September (the feast of the Exaltation of the Holy Cross) until Easter, a penance the rule once demanded all year until it made them ill.
quote: wear drugget chemises for six months in the year

text: Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582), the Spanish mystic who reformed the Carmelites. The story Hugo tells, of her refusing a would-be nun who was 'attached' to her Bible, is quoted for the rule against owning or loving any object, even a holy one.
quote: “Ah, you are attached to something! In that case, do not enter our order!”

text: Nuns of the Order of the Visitation, founded in 1610 by Francis de Sales and Jeanne de Chantal, a gentler order than the Benedictines. Their greeting 'Ave Maria' / 'Gratia plena' ('Hail Mary' / 'full of grace') is contrasted with the Petit-Picpus 'Forever!'.
quote: Among the Visitandines the one who enters says: “Ave Maria,”

text: An old burial ground on the south-western edge of Paris, on land once belonging to the convent, where the nuns had leave to be buried in a corner of their own at nightfall. Since the city forbids burials inside the convent, this is their only concession.
quote: a special corner in the ancient Vaugirard cemetery, which was made of land which had formerly belonged to their community

text: The weekly assembly of a religious house, presided over by the prioress, where business is decided and faults confessed aloud. 'Chapter' also names the hall where it meets.
quote: Once a week the chapter assembles: the prioress presides

text: From the Latin culpa, fault: the penance of lying prostrate before the prioress during the office for a trivial offence (a broken glass, a wrong note) until she taps her foot. The nun imposes it on herself; Hugo also calls it the peccavi, 'I have sinned'.
quote: To make one’s coulpe means to prostrate one’s self flat on one’s face

text: The three stages of entering a convent: a postulant asks admission and lives under the rule on trial (here two to four years), a novice wears the habit in white and is trained (four years), and a professed nun has taken final vows, rarely before twenty-three or twenty-four.
quote: One is a postulant for two years at least, often for four; a novice for four.

text: The profession ceremony as the Petit-Picpus kept it: the novice comes crowned with roses in her finest dress, prostrates herself, is covered with a black pall while the office of the dead is sung, and the nuns answer one another that she is dead and alive in Christ. Taking the veil is staged as a funeral.
quote: “Our sister is dead;” and the other file responds … “Our sister is alive in Jesus Christ!”

text: Names of the boarding-school's pupils meant to signal rank: old French nobility, and Talbot, the family of the Earls of Shrewsbury, the most prominent Catholic house in England. The school took girls of 'noble and mostly wealthy families' and raised them to dread the world.
quote: an English girl bearing the illustrious Catholic name of Talbot

text: A pendant in the shape of a dove, emblem of the Holy Spirit, worn on the breast of the pupils' blue uniform. Convent schools dressed their girls in a distinctive colour with a devotional badge, as the Legion of Honour school at Écouen did.
quote: a Holy Spirit of silver gilt or of copper on their breast

text: The feast of Martha of Bethany, 29 July, patron of housekeepers and servants. On this and a few other great days the pupils were allowed to dress as nuns and keep the whole office, which they treated as a holiday.
quote: particularly Saint Martha’s day

term: Homer and Perrault; Hecuba and la Mère-Grand
text: Homer's epics and Charles Perrault's fairy tales (1697) stand for the grand and the homely; Hecuba is the grieving queen of Troy and la Mère-Grand the grandmother of Little Red Riding Hood. Hugo says the girls' laughter would have smoothed the wrinkles of all these ancestresses.
quote: Homer would have come thither to laugh with Perrault

text: Tyrant of Syracuse in the fourth century BC, a name every schoolgirl who studied ancient history knew. The 'big big girls' turn the stout portress Sister Agatha into Agathocles.
quote: called her Agathocles

term: The four nations of the Collège Mazarin
text: Cardinal Mazarin's college (the 'Quatre-Nations') was founded in 1661 for students from four provinces newly joined to France, and sorted them accordingly. The pupils borrow the idea: each belongs to a 'nation' named after the corner of the refectory she eats in, Spider, Caterpillar, Woodlouse or Cricket.
quote: as in the old College Mazarin to distinguish four nations

text: Napoleon founded a school at the château of Écouen in 1807 for daughters of members of the Legion of Honour and put it under Madame Campan, who had been first lady of the bedchamber to Marie-Antoinette and ran a famous girls' school. Hugo cites its procession ranks ('virgins', 'florists') as another convent-school custom.
quote: At the beginning of this century Écouen was one of those strict and graceful places

text: Polichinelle, the hunch-backed, stick-wielding puppet of French fairground shows (the ancestor of Punch). A small girl's 'poem' about Punchinello beating the cat and being put in prison is one of Hugo's specimens of children's talk in the cloister.
quote: It was Punchinello who bestowed it on the cat.

text: A folk prayer in rhythmic peasant French, half charm and half creed, promising paradise to whoever says it three times night and morning; versions of it were recited across rural France for centuries. Painted over the refectory door, it vanished under whitewash in 1827.
quote: this prayer, which was called the “white Paternoster,”

text: Latin: 'No one shall communicate our rules or constitutions to outsiders.' The convent's rule book was a single unprinted copy the pupils were forbidden to read, which is why stealing a look at it was such an adventure.
quote: Nemo regulas, seu constitutiones nostras, externis communicabit.

text: 'Rounds of water': the large varnished bowls on the bare refectory tables in which the pupils rinsed their own cups and cutlery. Throwing a scrap of bad meat into them was punished.
quote: These bowls were called ronds d’eau.

text: Hyacinthe-Louis de Quélen, Archbishop of Paris from 1821 to 1839, a nobleman and a favourite of the Restoration court. Only the archbishop may enter the convent, so his word over-rides the prioress, and a bold pupil's three days' leave cannot be refused.
quote: Quélen smiled and said, “What, my dear child, a day’s leave of absence! Three days if you like.

text: Auguste de Rohan-Chabot, Prince de Léon, a young widower of one of France's greatest houses who became a priest, vicar-general of Paris, then Archbishop of Besançon and a cardinal. His elegance made him a hero to the schoolgirls, and the mad Madame Albertine's cry of 'Ah! Auguste!' set the convent gossiping about who she had been.
quote: M. Le Duc de Rohan, peer of France, officer of the Red Musketeers in 1815

text: One of the two companies of mounted musketeers of the king's household, named for the colour of their horses, revived by Louis XVIII in 1814 for young nobles and disbanded in 1815. A former musketeer in a cassock is Hugo's shorthand for the Restoration's mixing of gallantry and devotion.
quote: He had been a mousquetaire

text: Latin, 'great ladies': the privilege by which women of the highest rank could enter a closed convent that admitted no one else. Two severe duchesses used it to terrify the boarding-school.
quote: in virtue of the privilege Magnates mulieres

text: An air from Boieldieu's comic opera 'The Caliph of Baghdad' (1800), in which Zétulbé is the heroine. Played every day on a flute somewhere in the Rue Droit-Mur, it gave sixteen-year-old recluses an imaginary lover; the player turned out to be a blind, penniless old émigré.
quote: “My Zétulbé, come reign o’er my soul,”

text: The third building of the Petit-Picpus enclosure, where aged nuns of orders dissolved by the Revolution lived out their days on a small state pension, each keeping her own rule. Hugo calls the medley of black, grey and white habits a 'harlequin convent'.
quote: a sort of harlequin convent

text: A small order of nuns whose convent had occupied the Petit-Picpus house early in the eighteenth century; by 1824 one old nun of the order survived, too poor to wear its white robe and scarlet scapular, which she displayed on a doll. Hugo's note that 'today there remains only a doll' is the whole chapter in miniature.
quote: a nun of Sainte-Aure, the only one of her order who had survived

text: Stéphanie-Félicité de Genlis (1746–1830), governess of the Orléans princes and a prolific novelist and moralist, in old age a fierce devotee. The Duc d'Orléans (her former pupil, who became King Louis-Philippe in 1830) got her a cell in the convent about 1820; she left because the garden had no shade.
quote: Madame de Genlis had made romances.

text: The traditional names of the two thieves crucified beside Christ, the penitent and the impenitent. Madame de Genlis's Latin verses naming them (with the variant Gesmas) were pasted in her cupboard as a charm against burglars, a superstition Hugo says the Knights Hospitaller shared.
quote: Dismas et Gesmas, media est divina potestas

text: A quarantine station where travellers and goods suspected of plague were isolated. Hugo calls the public door of the convent church a 'lazaretto entrance' because it admits outsiders without letting them come near, or even see, the nuns behind the curtain.
quote: The public was even admitted by a sort of lazaretto entrance on the street.

text: A seventeenth-century Benedictine nun and scholar who wrote lives of the saints of her order ('L'Année bénédictine'). The prioress, Mademoiselle de Blemeur in the world and Mother Innocente in religion, comes of the same family and shares the learning.
quote: author of Lives of the Saints of the Order of Saint-Benoît

text: A nun gives up her family name on profession and takes a new one, here often a mystery of Christ's life (Nativity, Presentation, Assumption) or a saint. Hugo prints both names for each mother, the Mademoiselle she was and the Mother she became, which is why the list reads like a roll of two worlds.
quote: Mother Sainte-Mechtilde (Mademoiselle Gauvain)

text: The French sugar island in the Indian Ocean now called Réunion. A young nun from there, descended from the Chevalier Roze who fought the Marseilles plague of 1720, is among the 'prettiest' in the house.
quote: a charming girl of three and twenty, who was from the Isle de Bourbon

text: Giuseppe Ceracchi, an Italian sculptor who made busts of Washington and Bonaparte and was guillotined in 1801 for a plot to kill the First Consul. That his sister is a Petit-Picpus nun who went mad is one of Hugo's glimpses of the Revolution's wreckage inside the cloister.
quote: Mother Sainte-Céligne (sister of the sculptor Ceracchi), who went mad

text: Because the rule of silence forbids speech, a loud bell by the portress calls every person and announces every event by a code of strokes: one-one for the prioress, six-five for lessons, nineteen for the opening of the iron 'door of seclusion' when the archbishop comes. The pupils say 'to go to six-five', not 'to go to lessons'.
quote: a sort of acoustic telegraph

text: A French idiom, 'it's the devil by fours', meaning a great to-do. Madame de Genlis's bell signal was four-four, so the uncharitable had their pun ready whenever it rang.
quote: “C’est le diable a quatre,”—it’s the very deuce—said the uncharitable

term: Tennis-ground of the eleven thousand devils
text: A jeu de paume, the walled court of the old French game from which tennis descends, that stood on the convent's site from the fourteenth to the sixteenth century. Hugo likes the irony that a house of perpetual prayer was built on the 'eleven thousand devils'.
quote: the “tennis-ground of the eleven thousand devils.”

text: Hugo describes the convent's ground plan as the shape of a gallows (the French potence, an L or T) lying on the ground: the long arm along the Rue Droit-Mur, the short arm on the Rue Petit-Picpus. The image is chosen; the convent is a place of voluntary execution of the self.
quote: outlined, with considerable exactness, a gibbet laid flat on the ground

text: A great medieval abbey in Anjou, unusual in that an abbess ruled both monks and nuns; it was so large that, as the centenarian says, it had streets. Suppressed in the Revolution, it became a prison under Napoleon.
quote: She told wonders of the Abbey of Fontevrault—that it was like a city

text: Miromesnil was Keeper of the Seals (minister of justice) under Louis XVI from 1774 to 1787. A 'Presidentess' (présidente) was the wife of a président of one of the old parlements, the sovereign law courts. Dropping these names is the old nun's way of saying she was once in society.
quote: M. de Miromesnil, Keeper of the Seals under Louis XVI and of a Presidentess Duplat

text: A pre-Revolutionary ceremony of Burgundy and Champagne: a visiting grandee was offered four silver cups labelled monkey wine, lion wine, sheep wine and hog wine, the four stages of drunkenness (merry, quarrelsome, dull, brutish). The centenarian's stories are Hugo's way of letting the eighteenth century speak inside the cloister.
quote: monkey wine; on the second, lion wine; on the third, sheep wine; on the fourth, hog wine

text: A dish of painted tin-glazed earthenware from Faenza in Italy (the origin of the word 'faience'). The centenarian's secret treasure is a comic one showing cupids chased by apothecary boys with enema syringes, the sort of joke Molière built a play on.
quote: It was a Faenza platter representing little Loves flitting away pursued by apothecary lads armed with enormous syringes.

text: The walled enclosure of the medieval Knights Templar in north-east Paris, which gave its name to the quarter. Its convent of Benedictines of the Perpetual Adoration, with its famous chestnut tree and a comfortable parlour, is Hugo's foil to the grim Petit-Picpus; its tower, where Louis XVI was imprisoned, had been pulled down in 1808.
quote: At the convent of the Rue du Temple, in particular

text: Mother Mechtilde of the Blessed Sacrament (1614–1698), the Benedictine nun who founded the order of the Perpetual Adoration in Paris in 1653 after two sacrilegious thefts of the consecrated Host in 1649 scandalised the city. Two noblewomen endowed the first house in the Rue Cassette.
quote: Mother Catherine de Bar, called of the Holy Sacrament

text: The dowry a woman needed to enter the new order: an income of 300 livres a year, meaning a capital of 6,000 livres at five per cent. The livre was the pre-Revolutionary unit replaced by the franc of roughly equal value; religious houses lived on such dowries.
quote: unless she contributed three hundred livres income, which amounts to six thousand livres, to the principal

text: The paperwork of founding a convent under the old monarchy: the king's open letters granting permission, registered by the Chamber of Accounts (which audited royal finances) and the Parlement of Paris (the sovereign court). Hugo traces the order's 'legal consecration' step by step.
quote: all the rest, abbatial charter, and royal letters, was confirmed in 1654 by the Chamber of Accounts and the Parliament

text: A short letter of the Pope, less formal than a bull, granting a favour or permission. Alexander VII's brief of 1657 allowed the Petit-Picpus nuns to adopt the Perpetual Adoration while remaining a separate order.
quote: Pope Alexander VII had authorized, by a special brief

text: Latin, 'they have flown away'. Hugo uses it for the vanished schoolgirls of the Petit-Picpus; it is also the title of one of Goya's Caprichos, a woman borne off through the air.
quote: the latter had taken their departure. Volaverunt.

term: 'Hic jaceo. Vixi annos viginti et tres'
text: 'Here I lie. I lived twenty-three years': the epitaph of Julia Alpinula, a young Roman priestess said to have died of grief after failing to save her father. The inscription was a Renaissance forgery, but it was famous, and Hugo gives it to a nun dead at twenty-three.
quote: “Hic jaceo. Vixi annos viginti et tres.”

text: Latin, 'a garden enclosed', from the Song of Songs ('A garden enclosed is my sister, my spouse'), long applied to the Virgin and to the cloister. Hugo uses it to name the closed world he has just described.
quote: It is the closed garden, hortus conclusus.

text: The Savoyard counter-revolutionary philosopher (1753–1821) whose 'Soirées de Saint-Pétersbourg' praises the executioner as the keystone of social order. Hugo sets himself between de Maistre's 'hosanna' and Voltaire's sneer: respecting the convent without approving it.
quote: the hosanna of Joseph de Maistre, who wound up by anointing the executioner

text: Jean Calas, a Protestant merchant of Toulouse, was broken on the wheel in 1762 on a false charge of murdering his son; Voltaire's campaign cleared his name and made him the emblem of judicial fanaticism. Hugo's point is that the defender of Calas would have defended Jesus, 'the assassinated sage'.
quote: Voltaire would have defended Jesus as he defended Calas

text: Terms of the Ottoman harem: the seraglio is the sultan's palace of women, an odalisque a woman kept in it, the kislar-aga the chief black eunuch who guards it. Hugo uses them for the Spanish convent, with the archbishop as eunuch-guardian of 'souls reserved for God'.
quote: The archbishop, the kislar-aga of heaven, locked up and kept watch over this seraglio of souls

text: A monastic dungeon, from the formula vade in pace ('go in peace') said over a monk or nun walled up for life. Hugo describes the ones he saw himself at the ruined abbey of Villers near Brussels: stone boxes half under water, too short to lie in and too low to stand in.
quote: The in pace replaced the leather sack.

text: The Ottoman punishment of sewing a condemned woman of the harem into a sack and throwing her into the Bosphorus. Hugo's 'monstrous parallel' is that the East drowned what the West buried alive.
quote: That which was cast into the sea in the East was thrown into the ground in the West.

text: The three great judicial causes Voltaire fought in the 1760s: Calas executed for a murder he did not commit, the Chevalier de La Barre beheaded at nineteen for impiety, the Protestant Sirven condemned for his daughter's death. Hugo names them against those who call such protests mere 'declamations'.
quote: Voltaire on Calas, Labarre, and Sirven, declaimers

text: The Assyrian general beheaded by Judith in the Book of Judith. Pitying him, like calling Nero a victim or Tacitus a declaimer, is Hugo's parody of the fashionable rehabilitation of tyrants.
quote: pity is decidedly due to “that poor Holofernes.”

text: The old medical name for consumption, tuberculosis of the lungs, a wasting disease. Hugo calls monasticism 'a sort of phthisis for civilization': it depopulates and stops life short.
quote: is a sort of phthisis for civilization

text: Latin, 'the chalked ox'. Roman soothsayers who lacked a white victim rubbed a black heifer with chalk; Hugo's image for restorers who whitewash the past under names like 'social order' and 'legitimacy'.
quote: “She is white, Bos cretatus.”

term: Fakirs, bonzes, santons, marabouts, talapoins, dervishes
text: Holy men of other religions: Hindu and Muslim ascetics (fakirs), Buddhist monks of China and Japan (bonzes), Muslim hermits of Turkey and North Africa (santons, marabouts), Buddhist monks of Siam (talapoins), Sufi mendicants (dervishes). Hugo's quarrel is with ascetic seclusion everywhere, not with Catholic convents alone.
quote: fakirs, bonzes, santons, Greek monks, marabouts, talapoins, and dervishes

term: The city of '89 and of 1830 and of 1848
text: Paris named by its three revolutions: 1789, the July Revolution of 1830 that replaced Charles X with Louis-Philippe, and February 1848 that made the Second Republic. Hugo writes from after all three; a cloister in such a city is, he says, an anachronism.
quote: in the very heart of the city of ’89 and of 1830 and of 1848

text: The three words of the republican motto. Hugo argues that a monastery already realises two of them (all equal, all brothers) and lacks only the third; add liberty, that is, make entry and exit free, and the cloister becomes a republic.
quote: The monastery is the product of the formula: Equality, Fraternity. Oh! how grand is liberty!

term: A metaphysical school of the North
text: German idealist philosophy, which put 'Will' at the root of things (Schopenhauer's 'The World as Will and Idea' is the obvious target). Hugo's objection is that a school willing to say 'the plant wills' while denying a will in the universe has its logic backwards.
quote: replacing the word Force with the word Will

text: The doctrine that nothing is real or knowable, so that everything is 'a mental conception'. The word was new in 1862, popularised that year by Turgenev's 'Fathers and Sons'; Hugo answers it with 'Zero does not exist. Everything is something.'
quote: The negation of the infinite leads straight to nihilism.

text: The Lyceum was Aristotle's school in Athens. Hugo wants philosophy to turn man from a creature of happiness (Adam, Eden) into one of wisdom (Socrates, Marcus Aurelius): the garden of innocence should become a school.
quote: Eden should be changed into a Lyceum.

text: Four types of bad authority: Caiaphas the high priest who condemned Jesus, Draco the Athenian whose laws were 'written in blood', Trimalchio the vulgar millionaire of Petronius's Satyricon (here made a legislator), and the tyrant-emperor Tiberius. Fighting these, Hugo says, is the plain duty of history and philosophy.
quote: to combat Caiphas the High-priest, Draco the Lawgiver, Trimalcion the Legislator, Tiberius the Emperor

text: Life in a religious community under a common rule, as opposed to the hermit's solitude; from the Greek for 'common life'. Hugo treats the right to live apart in this way as a real human problem, not a joke.
quote: Cenobitism is a human problem.

text: A loan repayable only after someone's death, usually against an expected inheritance. Hugo's financial metaphors (a bill drawn on death, hell accepted as a post-obit on paradise) describe the convent as a bargain that pays out only beyond the grave.
quote: hell is accepted in advance as a post obit on paradise

text: The Greek thinker of the sixth century BC counted as the first philosopher. The legend that he stood motionless for four years is Hugo's proof that contemplation is labour: 'folded arms toil, clasped hands work'.
quote: Thales remained motionless for four years. He founded philosophy.

term: The Abbé de la Trappe replies to Horace
text: Rancé, the seventeenth-century reformer of the Trappist monks, whose rule meditates constantly on death, set against the Roman poet of 'seize the day'. Hugo's 'We must die' is the monk's answer to the poet, and he says sage and ascetic agree on it.
quote: “We must die.” The Abbé de la Trappe replies to Horace.

text: 'Voltaire erected this to God', the inscription the great sceptic put on the church he built at Ferney in 1761, pointedly dedicating it to God rather than to a saint. For Hugo it shows that even the mocker of religions could adore.
quote: Leibnitz praying is grand, Voltaire adoring is fine. Deo erexit Voltaire.

text: A legal officer who draws up deeds, contracts and wills, a respectable small-town profession. Fauchelevent was one before he failed and sank to carting, which is why Hugo says his peasant cunning has a notary's trickery and good grammar in it.
quote: He was a peasant, but he had been a notary

text: Hugo's remark that peasants of Picardy and the north kept 'an old fund of Bonapartism': loyalty to the Emperor who had ended feudal dues and filled the armies with their sons. Fauchelevent is pleased rather than shocked to think M. Madeleine may be in hiding for a political affair.
quote: had an old fund of Bonapartism about him

term: The prayers of the forty hours
text: A devotion of continuous prayer before the exposed Host for forty hours, the time Christ's body lay in the tomb, here offered for a dying nun. With the whole community absorbed in it, no one is looking toward the gardener's hut.
quote: The prayers of the forty hours are being said.

text: The convent's death-bell: one stroke a minute for twenty-four hours, from the death until the body leaves the church. Fauchelevent reads every peal of the house, and interprets for Valjean each stage of 'the ceremony of dying' as it rings.
quote: The bell will continue to strike once a minute for twenty-four hours

text: The médecin des morts, a physician employed by the municipality to view every corpse and certify death before burial was permitted. He is the one man besides the gardener who may enter the convent's dead-room, and the nuns dislike his visit because 'he lifts the veil'.
quote: the dead-doctor is to come here and view a corpse

text: 'Out of the depths', the opening of Psalm 130, the psalm sung at burials. Fauchelevent ends his account of how a nun goes to heaven in a hearse with the words a priest says over a grave.
quote: That’s what a burial is like. De profundis.

text: Jean Mabillon (1632–1707), the great Benedictine scholar who founded the critical study of documents and edited Saint Bernard, and Horstius, an earlier editor who printed fewer of Bernard's letters. The prioress's point, that one does not despise the lesser worker, is her way of telling Fauchelevent to manage with a woman's help.
quote: Dom Mabillon gives four hundred and seventeen epistles of Saint Bernard, while Merlonus Horstius only gives three hundred and sixty-seven

text: A follower of the austere Catholic movement, centred on Port-Royal, that stressed predestination and was condemned by Rome; by 1824 it was a stubborn minority. A Jansenist lady 'turned orthodox' merely by seeing Mother Crucifixion at prayer is offered as proof of the dead nun's sanctity.
quote: Madame de Béthune, a Jansenist, turned orthodox

term: Cardinal de Bérulle dying at mass
text: Pierre de Bérulle, founder of the French Oratory, died in 1629 while saying mass, at the words 'Hanc igitur oblationem' ('This offering, therefore'). The prioress ranks Mother Crucifixion's death just below this ideal.
quote: while pronouncing these words: Hanc igitur oblationem

text: Pope from 1800 to 1823, Pius VII came to Paris to crown Napoleon in 1804 and was later held prisoner by him. Fauchelevent's slip, catching 'Emperor' and correcting to 'Bonaparte', is a Bonapartist's reflex in a royalist house.
quote: “The one who crowned the Emp—Bonaparte.”

text: The prioress's precedents for obeying a dead saint's wish about burial: a bishop whose tomb says only 'worm', an abbot buried under the gallows, a bishop who asked to be spat on, and Bernard Gui the Dominican inquisitor carried from Spain to Limoges. Real and doubtful lore mixed, cited from obscure chroniclers; Hugo is enjoying her erudition and her obstinacy at once.
quote: Acarus, which signifies, a worm of the earth

text: 'The cross stands while the world turns', the motto of the Carthusian order. The prioress answers every mention of the police inspector with a Latin tag, and Fauchelevent answers every Latin tag with 'Amen'.
quote: Stat crux dum volvitur orbis.

text: The prioress's torrent is accurate: Bernard of Clairvaux founded scores of monasteries, defeated the philosopher Abelard at the council of Sens in 1140, denounced the monk Raoul who incited massacres of Jews, advised popes and kings, wrote the rule of the Templars and preached the Second Crusade. 'Two hundred and fifty miracles' is her own addition.
quote: he overthrew Abeilard at the council of Sens in 1140

term: Father Coton and Henri IV's oath
text: Pierre Coton, Jesuit confessor to Henri IV, is remembered because the king, told not to swear 'je renie Dieu' (I deny God), substituted 'jarnicoton', a nonsense oath on the priest's name. The prioress complains that people know this and not that Coton helped found the Oratory.
quote: because he furnished Henri IV, the Huguenot king, with the material for an oath

text: Martin of Tours, the fourth-century soldier-saint, cut his cloak in two to clothe a beggar at Amiens, the best-known act of charity in French hagiography. The prioress sets it against the scandal of bad bishops.
quote: Martin de Tours from being a saint, and giving half of his cloak to a beggar

text: César de Bus (1544–1607) founded the Fathers of Christian Doctrine to teach catechism to the poor; Voltaire needs no introduction. That the world knows the mocker and not the teacher is, for the prioress, the whole indictment of the age.
quote: The name of Voltaire is known, but not the name of César de Bus.

term: The Emperor Henry II, the Saint and the Lame
text: Henry II of Germany (died 1024), the only German emperor canonised, who fought an antipope and restored Benedict VIII; he was also lame. The prioress offers him as comfort to the limping gardener, who hears 'two surtouts' (overcoats) and agrees.
quote: has two surnames, the Saint and the Lame

text: The municipal public-health authority that, with the commissary of police and the prefecture, regulated burials in Paris and forbade interment inside churches and convents. Fauchelevent raises each in turn; the prioress dismisses them all as 'a revolutionary invention'.
quote: Your sanitary department is a revolutionary invention.

text: Hugo cites a monk Castillejo for the tale that the Emperor Charles V, after abdicating in 1556 to the monastery of Yuste, had a woman he loved ('the Plombes') smuggled in and out in a coffin. No such source is known; the point is that Valjean's convict's trick has, Hugo claims, an imperial precedent.
quote: If we are to credit the monk Austin Castillejo

text: A small hand tool for boring holes in wood. Valjean asks for a few gimlet holes near his mouth and the lid nailed on loosely, the practical details of being buried alive on purpose.
quote: You surely must have a gimlet, you will make a few holes here and there

text: 'The Good Quince', the wine-shop beside the Vaugirard cemetery with a quince painted on its sign, one wall on the drinkers' tables and the other on the tombs. Fauchelevent's whole plan rests on getting the gravedigger inside it before the gates close.
quote: ‘Come and drink a bout while the Bon Coing is open.’

text: A permit issued by the department of public funerals that let a gravedigger out of a Paris cemetery after the gates shut at sunset: he dropped it in the porter's box and the small gate opened. Without it he must be identified and fined fifteen francs. The Vaugirard, where the nuns were buried at nightfall, ran on this card.
quote: his gravedigger’s card furnished by the department of public funerals

text: The carriage gate and the foot gate, the old names the quarter kept for the cemetery's two entrances beside the keeper's lodge built by Perronet, the engineer of the Pont de la Concorde.
quote: still called the porte cavalière and the porte piétonne

text: The great landscaped cemetery opened in 1804 on the eastern heights of Paris, which by the 1820s was the fashionable place to be buried. To be buried at the Vaugirard 'hinted at poverty'; Père-Lachaise 'is equivalent to having furniture of mahogany'.
quote: to be buried in Père-Lachaise is equivalent to having furniture of mahogany

text: Gribier's grim joke on succession: as the king replaced the emperor in 1814, so he replaces Father Mestienne. It is the first blow to Fauchelevent, whose plan assumed a drunkard he knew.
quote: “After Napoleon, Louis XVIII. After Mestienne, Gribier.

text: Cheap, sour red wines from villages just outside Paris, the drink of the barriers; Fauchelevent calls a jug of Suresnes 'little Father Lenoir' and offers Argenteuil at six sous. Gribier, who never drinks, is unmoved by either.
quote: It is a jug of Surêne, morbigou!

text: An écrivain public kept a stall where he wrote letters for people who could not; Gribier's is in the Umbrella Market in the Rue de Sèvres, where the cooks of the Croix-Rouge quarter dictate love letters to soldiers. 'In the morning I write love letters; in the evening I dig graves.'
quote: But I am still a public writer.

text: The Prytanée, the military college founded under the Revolution and Napoleon (at Saint-Cyr, then La Flèche) for sons of officers. Gribier's father was its porter and 'destined him for literature' before losing his money on the exchange.
quote: My father was a porter at the Prytaneum.

term: The quarter of an hour of Rabelais
text: The moment of paying the bill, from the story that Rabelais, penniless at an inn, got himself arrested as a poisoner to be carried to Paris free. Fauchelevent offers drinks but leaves the question of who pays carefully dark.
quote: the old gardener left the proverbial quarter of an hour named after Rabelais in the dark

text: What Valjean hears through the planks: 'Those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame' (Daniel 12:2); 'Eternal rest give unto him, O Lord' / 'And let perpetual light shine upon him'; 'May he rest in peace'. The holy water pattering on the lid follows.
quote: Requiem aeternam dona ei, Domine.

text: A raw recruit; Fauchelevent's name for the new gravedigger once he has the upper hand, as Gribier called him 'peasant' and 'villager'. The fine of fifteen francs, 'three pieces of a hundred sous', is more than a labourer earned in a week.
quote: “Ah, come now, conscript,” said Fauchelevent, “none of this despair.

text: A small town on the Somme near Amiens, in Picardy, Fauchelevent's own country. He gives it as the birthplace of his 'brother' Ultime, borrowing the name of a real brother who had died.
quote: “From Picquigny, near Amiens.”

text: The name under which Valjean is admitted to the convent as assistant gardener: that of Fauchelevent's dead brother, so the papers would hold if anyone looked. The nuns never use it, calling him 'the other Fauvent'.
quote: “Ultime Fauchelevent.” He really had had a brother named Ultime, who was dead.

text: From 'Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and unto God the things that are God's' (Matthew 22:21). Hugo's verdict on the double burial: the state's rules were dodged, the dead nun's wish fulfilled, and 'no one was aware of it'.
quote: eluded Caesar and satisfied God

text: 'Monsieur' is the title of the king's eldest brother, here the Comte d'Artois, who became Charles X in 1824. Jean-Baptiste de Latil, his confessor, became Archbishop of Reims and crowned him there in 1825, and was made a cardinal.
quote: M. de Latil, Monsieur’s confessor, afterwards Archbishop of Reims and Cardinal

text: Pope from 1823 to 1829, Annibale della Genga, a conservative who favoured the religious orders. Hugo's 'note' in which the Pope praises 'an excellent gardener, who is also a holy man, named Fauvent' is a comic invention capping the chapter.
quote: the then reigning Pope, Leo XII

text: The English pictorial weekly, founded in 1842, which printed engravings of prize cattle. Fauchelevent knowing nothing of his fame in Rome is like a Durham bull ignorant of its own portrait; the comparison is deliberately out of its time.
quote: whose portrait is published in the London Illustrated News

text: A girl taken into a fee-paying convent school without payment, as an act of charity and in hope of a vocation. The prioress's judgement that Cosette 'will grow up ugly' decides it: plain girls, Hugo observes, make nuns more readily than pretty ones.
quote: gave her a place in the school as a charity pupil

text: In 1793 the royalist peasants of the Vendée, in western France, rose against the Republic and issued their own notes 'in the king's name'; the Chouans were their guerrilla allies in Brittany and Maine. The old gardener who nailed such a note over the chimney was one of these royalist rebels, ending his days in a convent.
quote: This specimen of Vendean paper money had been nailed to the wall by the preceding gardener, an old Chouan

text: A strong-smelling resin used to keep moths from stored cloth. Valjean packs Cosette's little mourning suit, stockings and shoes in camphor and convent aromatics in a locked valise; she asks what is in the box that smells so good.
quote: with a quantity of camphor and all the aromatics in which convents abound

text: Joining a shoot or bud of a good fruit variety onto a wild rootstock so that the tree bears the better fruit. Valjean, once a tree-pruner in Faverolles, grafts the convent's wild orchard; it is honest skilled work and his way of being useful.
quote: He budded them and made them produce excellent fruit.

text: The Christian idea that the innocent may take on suffering to atone for the guilty, as Christ did; the nuns' 'reparation' for the sins of the world is its daily practice. Valjean, who understands a convict's expiation for himself, is stopped short by this other kind, and it humbles him.
quote: “The most divine of human generosities, the expiation for others.”

text: The Paris street boy: a child of seven to thirteen who lives more in the street than at home, ragged, cheeky, quick and free. The word was still new and slangy when Hugo wrote, and Hapgood keeps it, sometimes adding 'street arab', the English equivalent of the day. Book I of this volume is a portrait of the type rather than of any one child.
quote: the child is called the gamin

text: Latin, 'little man', a word used by the Roman comic playwright Plautus. Hugo likes to dress the gutter child in classical tags: the effect is half mock-heroic and half tender. He keeps calling the gamin 'the homuncio' in the chapters that follow.
quote: Homuncio, Plautus would say.

text: French has two words for 'you': the polite vous and the familiar tu ('thou'), kept for family, close friends, children and inferiors. A small boy who says tu to prostitutes ('gay women' in Victorian English) is claiming to be their equal and their pal. Hapgood often renders tu as 'thou' to keep the nuance.
quote: calls gay women “thou,”

text: Victorian English for a homeless or half-wild city child, from the idea of the wandering Bedouin. Hapgood uses it as a gloss on gamin; to Hugo's readers the French word carried more cheek and less pity.
quote: The gamin—the street arab—of Paris is the dwarf of the giant.

text: A translation of the French slang manger les pissenlits par la racine, 'to be dead and buried', still in use today, much like English 'pushing up daisies'. It is the first of the many street sayings Hugo collects in this book.
quote: to be dead is “to eat dandelions by the root;”

text: A pun on the Pont des Arts, the footbridge across the Seine by the Louvre, which charged a toll. In heavy rain gamins laid planks across flooded gutters and charged passers-by a sou to cross: their own toll bridge.
quote: which he calls “making the bridge of arts,”

text: French for 'rags'. Here it is the gamins' private currency, scraps of worked copper picked up in the street, which pass from hand to hand at a fixed value among the children.
quote: This curious money, which receives the name of loques—rags

text: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand (1754–1838), the bishop turned diplomat who served the Revolution, Napoleon, the Bourbons and Louis-Philippe in turn. He was famous for cynical one-liners. Hugo gives the gamin as many sayings as Talleyrand, and more honesty.
quote: this child has as many of them as Talleyrand

text: Parisian slang for a gamin at the theatre, perched in the cheapest seats under the roof. Hugo makes him the winged form of the street boy, as the moth is of the larva. The word survives as the name of the cheeky Paris urchin type.
quote: he was the street arab, he becomes the titi

text: The highest, cheapest gallery of a theatre, under the roof, was called le paradis in French, as 'the gods' in English. Hugo plays on the name: the stuffy, filthy 'keel' of the upturned ship becomes heaven because the children are happy there.
quote: the name of Paradise

text: Anne Boutet, called Mademoiselle Mars (1779–1847), the leading comic actress of the Comédie-Française for thirty years, admired for her elegance and diction. The gamins' nickname 'Muche' plays on se musser (to hide), mocking her as she aged in young roles.
quote: the popularity of Mademoiselle Mars

text: A nonsense refrain from old popular songs, like 'fol-de-rol'. Setting it beside 'Alleluia', as the Jack-pudding (the fairground clown) beside the De Profundis, is Hugo's way of saying the gamin mixes the sacred and the comic without blinking.
quote: tempers Alleluia with Matanturlurette

text: The giant spirit of the Cape of Good Hope in Camões's Portuguese epic 'The Lusiads' (1572), who rises from the storm to warn Vasco da Gama. Hugo's point: faced with an epic monster, the street boy would just call it a bogeyman.
quote: If Adamastor were to appear to him

text: Joseph Prudhomme is the pompous, platitudinous bourgeois invented by the caricaturist Henry Monnier in the 1830s, a byword for smug respectability. Fouillou stands for the poking, rummaging street child (fouiller means to rummage). Hugo pairs them as the two poles of Paris: the lounger who looks on and the gamin who acts.
quote: Prudhomme and Fouillou

text: From Horace's 'Art of Poetry': a potter sets out to make an amphora, but as the wheel turns (currit rota) out comes a mere jug. Hugo reverses the line: Paris starts with a jug of common clay and turns out an amphora. Ionian and Boeotian are the old Greek types of the refined and the dull.
quote: currit rota, the Spirit of Paris

text: Horace opens one of his Epistles by greeting his friend Fuscus, 'lover of the city', from himself, Flaccus, 'lover of the country'. Hugo gives the gamin both loves, which leads him into the waste ground around Paris.
quote: Urbis amator, like Fuscus; ruris amator, like Flaccus

text: The ring of half-rural land and villages just outside a French city's limits, beyond the toll barriers. Hugo calls it the 'limbo' of Paris, neither town nor country: quarries, market gardens, waste ground and cheap tea-gardens, where runaway children play.
quote: the banlieue of Paris is another

term: The wall of Grenelle 'speckled with balls'
text: The plain of Grenelle, south-west of the city by the Champ-de-Mars, was where military executions were carried out by firing squad; the wall behind the condemned was pocked with bullet marks. Hugo lists it among the bleak landmarks of the outskirts he roamed as a young man.
quote: the hideous wall of Grenelle all speckled with balls

text: Hapgood's English for the liard, the smallest copper coin of old France, worth a quarter of a sou. It was already out of use by the 1820s. The children quarrelling over them are quarrelling over almost nothing.
quote: quarrelling over half-farthings

term: 'The swallows of the bridge of Arcola'
text: A notorious band of homeless children who slept under the arches of the Pont d'Arcole, by the Hôtel de Ville, and lived by petty theft; their case caused a scandal in the 1840s. Hugo cites them as the darker side of the Paris street child.
quote: “the swallows of the bridge of Arcola.”

text: Jean-Baptiste Colbert, Louis XIV's great minister, built up the French navy in the 1660s, and the Mediterranean galleys needed rowers. Courts were urged to sentence as many men to the oar as possible: Protestants (Huguenots) for refusing a Catholic gesture such as baring the head to a procession, and vagrant boys of fifteen.
quote: Colbert had the commissioners of provinces and the parliaments make as many convicts as possible.

text: In 1750 a rumour ran through Paris that police were kidnapping children so that a sick Louis XV could bathe in their blood; riots broke out and several people were hanged. The lawyer Edmond Barbier recorded it in his journal. The exempts were police officers of the old regime.
quote: the king’s baths of purple. Barbier speaks ingenuously of these things

text: A short story Hugo himself published in 1834, about a starving workman jailed for theft who kills a cruel prison director and is guillotined. Hugo is drily claiming that the word gamin first got into print through his own pen.
quote: It is in a little work entitled “Claude Gueux” that this word made its appearance.

text: Samson was the family of hereditary Paris executioners who worked the guillotine from Louis XVI to the 1840s; the Abbé Montès was the prison chaplain who rode with the condemned in the cart. To the gamin they are celebrities, the stars of the show at the Place de Grève.
quote: Samson and the Abbé Montès are the truly popular names

text: Hugo's roll-call of men guillotined in Paris between about 1820 and 1840, as the street boys remember them. Lacenaire was a poet-murderer who became a romantic celebrity; Papavoine killed two children in 1824; Bories was one of the 'four sergeants of La Rochelle' executed for a political plot in 1822, hence the confusion of 'politicians' with assassins.
quote: In the brotherhood of gamins Voltaire is not known, but Papavoine is.

text: A rhetorical term for a striking exclamation that sums up what came before. Hugo uses the learned word, tongue in cheek, for a street boy's wish to see someone fall from a fifth-floor window.
quote: a profound epiphonema

text: In 1831 the caricaturist Charles Philipon drew King Louis-Philippe's heavy, jowly face turning by stages into a pear, and the pear became the opposition's emblem; street boys chalked pears on every wall. In Hugo's anecdote the king himself finishes a child's pear and pays him a louis, with a pun on the king's face being on the coin too.
quote: from 1830 to 1848, he scrawled pears on the walls

text: Evoe, the ecstatic cry of the worshippers of Bacchus in Greek ritual. Hugo mock-solemnly hears it, and the chants of the Panathenaea (Athens's great festival), in the gamins' warning cry when the police come for the boys bathing in the Seine.
quote: one encounters again the ancient Evohe

text: In Greek myth, a king punished in the underworld by standing in water that drains away when he stoops to drink, under fruit that the wind lifts out of reach. 'To play Tantalus' is to long for something forever just out of reach: here, overthrowing the government and getting one's trousers mended.
quote: There are two things to which he plays Tantalus

text: The Pope's ambassador to a foreign court, resident in Paris in the Rue de l'Université. The anticlerical gamin thumbs his nose at the gate simply because 'there is a curé there'.
quote: It was there, in fact, that the Papal Nuncio lived.

text: Jean-Baptiste Poquelin is Molière (1622–1673), France's great comic playwright, son of a Paris upholsterer near the market of Les Halles. Beaumarchais (1732–1799), the watchmaker's son who wrote 'The Barber of Seville' and 'The Marriage of Figaro', mocked the nobility with street-wise cheek. Hugo claims both for the gamin's line.
quote: There was something of that boy in Poquelin

text: Desmoulins was the young journalist who roused the Paris crowd at the Palais-Royal two days before the fall of the Bastille in 1789. General Championnet, a Revolutionary soldier who took Naples in 1799, was said to have forced the clergy there to make the blood of Saint Januarius liquefy on schedule: Hugo's 'treated miracles brutally'.
quote: Camille Desmoulins was a native of the faubourgs

text: Joseph Bara, a boy of thirteen or fourteen serving with the Republican army, killed by Vendéan rebels in 1793; legend says he died crying 'Vive la République' rather than surrender horses. The Republic made him a hero and painters made him an icon. Hugo makes him the gamin turned hero.
quote: Barra the drummer-boy was a gamin of Paris

text: The war-horse of the Book of Job (39:25), which 'saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smelleth the battle afar off'. Hugo sets the boy's 'Forward!' beside it. The 'little Theban' who shakes off the lion's skin is the young Hercules.
quote: as the horse of Scripture says “Vah!”

text: Latin, 'little Greek': the Roman sneer for the quick-witted, rootless Greeks who lived by their wits in imperial Rome, as tutors, flatterers and jacks-of-all-trades (Juvenal's satire is the classic portrait). Hugo makes the gamin the Paris equivalent: the child of an old civilization, born knowing.
quote: like the graeculus of Rome in days gone by

text: This chapter is a dizzying catalogue matching every piece of ancient Rome and Greece with something in modern Paris: the Faubourg Saint-Antoine is the Aventine, the hill of the Roman plebs; the Gemonian stairs, where the bodies of the executed were thrown, are replaced by ridicule. Most of the Latin names come from Plautus, Horace and Juvenal. The reader needs none of them to follow the point: everything that ever existed elsewhere exists in Paris.
quote: Paris has a capital, the Town-Hall, a Parthenon, Notre-Dame, a Mount Aventine, the Faubourg Saint-Antoine

text: Paris slang for the underworld of petty thieves, set here beside the lazzarone, the idle street poor of Naples. Faraud, in the same list, is a swaggering dandy of the lower classes, the Paris version of the Spanish majo.
quote: its lazzarone is the pègre

text: Three famous impostors or wonder-workers of the late eighteenth century in Paris. Franz Mesmer treated patients round a tub of 'magnetised' water; Cagliostro was a Sicilian adventurer who sold elixirs and séances; the Comte de Saint-Germain claimed to be centuries old. Hugo matches them with the oracles and magicians of antiquity.
quote: The vat of Trophonius contains nothing that is not in Mesmer’s tub

text: In the 1720s and 1730s crowds of Jansenist devotees gathered at the tomb of the deacon Pâris in the Saint-Médard churchyard, falling into convulsions and claiming miraculous cures, until the king had the cemetery closed. A wit chalked on the gate: 'By order of the King, God is forbidden to work miracles here.'
quote: the cemetery of Saint-Médard works quite as good miracles

text: Mayeux was a lewd, boastful hunchback, a stock figure of 1830s caricature and street songs. Marie-Anne Lenormand was the most celebrated fortune-teller of Paris, said to have read the cards for Josephine and Napoleon. Hugo casts them as Paris's Aesop and its witch Canidia.
quote: Paris has an Aesop-Mayeux, and a Canidia, Mademoiselle Lenormand

text: The spiritualist craze that reached Paris from America in 1853, when people sat round tables waiting for spirits to tilt them and rap out messages. Hugo himself held séances of this kind in exile on Jersey, so his comparison with the oracle of Dodona is not entirely mocking.
quote: it makes tables turn as Dodona did tripods

text: A Bordeaux gentleman who, after quarrelling with the Bourbons he had served, paraded the arcades of the Palais-Royal for decades in filthy rags, unshaven, refusing all help, until his death in 1842. He was one of the famous sights of Restoration Paris: a beggar with the bearing of a lord.
quote: makes Chodruc Duclos

text: Two stage hypocrites. Tartuffe is Molière's sanctimonious impostor (1664), who uses piety to swindle his host; Basile is the oily music-master in Beaumarchais's 'Barber of Seville', famous for his speech on how slander grows. Paris, says Hugo, enjoys them both too much to be shocked.
quote: it does not hold its nose before Basile

term: The bal Mabile and the lorette
text: The bal Mabille was an open-air dance hall off the Champs-Élysées, fashionable from the 1840s. A lorette was a kept woman of the new quarter round the church of Notre-Dame-de-Lorette, a step up from the working grisette. The Barrière du Combat was where animal fights were staged for paying crowds.
quote: the dealer in ladies’ wearing apparel there devours the lorette with her eyes

term: The oath of tennis; the night of the 4th of August
text: Two founding moments of the Revolution of 1789. On 20 June the deputies of the Third Estate, locked out of their hall at Versailles, swore in a royal tennis court not to separate until France had a constitution. On the night of 4 August the Assembly abolished feudal privileges in a single sitting.
quote: it forces all nations to take the oath of tennis

text: Hugo's roll of liberators lit by the French example: the American, Polish and South American independence leaders; Markos Botsaris and Kanaris of the Greek war against the Turks; Rafael del Riego, whose rising at the Isle de Léon near Cádiz in 1820 forced a constitution on Spain; the revolutionaries of 1848 at Pest and Venice; Garibaldi at Palermo in 1860; and John Brown at Harper's Ferry in 1859. Byron died at Missolonghi in 1824 while helping the Greeks.
quote: Washington, Kosciusko, Bolivar, Bozzaris, Riego, Bem, Manin, Lopez, John Brown, Garibaldi

text: Two jokes of Paris art students: the painter Bouginier had an enormous nose, and his fellow students caricatured it on walls wherever they went, reportedly as far as the ruins of Greece; 'Crédeville voleur' was a similar running gag scrawled on monuments. Even when Paris is conquering the world with ideas, says Hugo, it is still a gamin with a stick of charcoal.
quote: sketches in charcoal Bouginier’s nose on the wall of the temple of Theseus

text: François-Marie Arouet was Voltaire's real name. The list of thinkers who 'prepared' the Revolution (Montesquieu, Diderot, Beaumarchais, Condorcet, Voltaire, Rousseau) ends with Danton, the orator who 'dared' it: Hugo's praise of audacity over theory.
quote: that Arouet should prepare it

text: Latin, 'let there be light', God's first command in Genesis (1:3). Light is Hugo's word, all through these chapters, for education and progress.
quote: The cry: Audacity! is a Fiat lux.

text: Cicero's contemptuous name for the Roman poor, 'the dregs of the city', and Edmund Burke, the British statesman whose 'Reflections on the Revolution in France' (1790) spoke of the 'swinish multitude'. Hugo throws back the insults and asks why the barefoot poor should be abandoned for not knowing how to read.
quote: “Fex urbis,” exclaims Cicero; “mob,” adds Burke

text: A hill north-east of Paris where the great medieval gibbet stood, and which later held the city's horse-knackers' yards and refuse dumps, notorious for stench and rats. The 'knacker of Montfaucon' and the porter of La Râpée, the wine and timber wharf on the Seine, are the two ends of the working poor.
quote: the knacker of Montfaucon

text: The marching song written in 1792 and carried to Paris by volunteers from Marseilles, adopted as the national anthem of the Republic. Under the Restoration it was banned as seditious; to sing it was to declare for revolution.
quote: sing the Marseillaises

text: The boulevard on the north-eastern side of Paris lined with popular theatres, circuses and puppet shows, nicknamed the 'Boulevard of Crime' for the melodramas played there. The Cirque (Franconi's equestrian circus) and the Porte Saint-Martin theatre stood nearby, and the Château-d'Eau was a big fountain at the end of the boulevard. It is the natural home of a theatre-loving gamin.
quote: people noticed on the Boulevard du Temple, and in the regions of the Château-d’Eau

text: Hugo's way of moving the clock: the second part ended with events of 1823–24, so the story now stands in about 1831–32. He has just spent the whole book on the gamin as a type before introducing one particular boy.
quote: Eight or nine years after the events narrated in the second part of this story

term: 'A Pole or an Italian, or even a Spaniard'
text: After the failed risings in Poland, Italy and Spain around 1830–31, political refugees poured into Paris, and charities and the government gave them relief. A destitute lodger who says he will answer to any of these nationalities is telling the portress he means to beg under whatever story pays best.
quote: if anyone should chance to come and inquire for a Pole or an Italian, or even a Spaniard, perchance, it is I

text: The two lowest trades of Paris. The égoutier cleaned out the city's drains; the chiffonnier went through the rubbish at night with a basket and a hook, collecting rags for the paper mills, bones and scraps to sell. Hugo puts them at the very bottom of the social ladder the Gorbeau tenants are sliding down.
quote: the sewer-man who sweeps up the mud, and the ragpicker who collects scraps

term: Streets named for provinces and capitals
text: The streets round the Temple were laid out under Louis XIV and named after French provinces (Normandie, Saintonge, Poitou, Bretagne). In Hugo's own day the new 'Tivoli' or Europe quarter near the Gare Saint-Lazare got streets named after European capitals (Rome, Londres, Vienne). His 'progression in which progress is visible' is a small joke about a nation widening its horizons.
quote: the streets of the new Tivoli quarter have received the names of all the capitals of Europe

text: M. Gillenormand calls himself ruined on an income of 15,000 francs, when a labourer earned perhaps 500 a year and a clerk 1,500: he is comfortably rich by any ordinary measure. His dream of 'a hundred thousand livres income' is the fortune of a great lord. The old man still counts in livres, the money of the old regime, roughly equal to the franc.
quote: All he had left, in fact, was an income of about fifteen thousand francs.

text: Le Grand Siècle: the reign of Louis XIV (1643–1715), the age of Versailles, when a gentleman might beat a servant or an impudent commoner with his cane. M. Gillenormand, born in the 1740s, keeps its manners into the 1830s.
quote: he beat people as he had done in the great century

text: An old French insult, 'carrion', used to abuse women and servants: roughly 'you hussy' or 'you wretch'. His oath 'by the pantoufloche of the pantouflochade' is nonsense built on pantoufle, slipper: an old man's comic swearing.
quote: “Ah! carogne!”

text: The old aristocratic quarter of the right bank around the Place Royale (now Place des Vosges) and the Temple, full of seventeenth-century mansions. By the 1820s the nobility had moved west to the Faubourg Saint-Germain and the Marais had become a quiet backwater of old bourgeois and retired families, a fitting home for a relic like M. Gillenormand.
quote: He lived in the Marais, Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6.

text: The Gobelins in Paris and the Beauvais works were the royal tapestry manufactories, whose pastoral scenes covered the walls and chairs of rich eighteenth-century houses. Coromandel lacquer was carved, painted Chinese lacquer named after the Indian coast through which it was traded. M. Gillenormand's rooms are a museum of his youth.
quote: furnished to the very ceilings with great Gobelins and Beauvais tapestries representing pastoral scenes
