text: Louis-Victor de Rochechouart, Duc de Vivonne (1636–1688), General of the Galleys under Louis XIV and brother of the king's mistress Madame de Montespan. Hugo's detail that the straw hangings of the boudoir were woven by galley-slaves to order for a nobleman's mistress is pointed.
quote: made on the galleys of Louis XIV and ordered of his convicts by M. de Vivonne for his mistress

text: Jacob Jordaens (1593–1678), the Flemish painter of Antwerp, Rubens's follower, known for big, boisterous, fleshy canvases of feasts and peasants. A Jordaens portrait marks M. Gillenormand as a real connoisseur.
quote: painted by Jordaens

text: The dandies of 1795–99, after the Terror, who wore huge lapels, tight breeches, high cravats and swallowtail coats, and affected a lisp that dropped the letter r ('incoyable!'). M. Gillenormand stopped following fashion then, so in the 1830s he still dresses like a fop of thirty-five years before.
quote: it was that of the Incroyables of the Directory

text: A small pocket in the waistband of breeches, made for a watch. A man who 'always thrust his hands into his fobs' strikes the pose of a self-satisfied old beau.
quote: He always thrust his hands into his fobs.

term: The Camargo, the Sallé, the Guimard
text: The great ballerinas of the eighteenth-century Paris Opéra. Marie Camargo and Marie Sallé were rivals of the 1730s, both praised in Voltaire's verses; Marie-Madeleine Guimard was the star of the 1770s and 80s, famous for her lovers and her mansion. M. Gillenormand's memories run from one to the other.
quote: the Camargo and the Sallé

text: Every Holy Week in the eighteenth century, fashionable Paris drove out to the abbey of Longchamp in the Bois de Boulogne, nominally for the services, in fact to show off carriages and the season's clothes. M. Gillenormand's description of the Guimard there is a string of comic fashion names of the day.
quote: the last time I saw her at Longchamps

text: Probably the Comtesse de Boufflers (1725–1800), the brilliant hostess of the Temple circle and friend of Rousseau and Hume, whose verdict could make or mar a young man in society. 'A charming fool' is a very eighteenth-century compliment.
quote: Madame de Boufflers, having seen him by chance when he was twenty

text: Politicians of the Restoration and the July Monarchy: Corbière was Charles X's ultra-royalist interior minister, Humann a finance minister from Alsace, and Casimir Périer the banker who led Louis-Philippe's government in 1831–32. To M. Gillenormand, all are vulgar upstarts, whatever their party.
quote: Corbière! Humann! Casimir Périer!

text: Eighteenth-century French poetry avoided plain words for genteel circumlocutions (a cow was 'the heifer of the plain', a fiddle 'the sonorous wood'). Hugo, who had led the Romantic revolt against that style, notes that the same age was frankly coarse in conversation.
quote: the age of periphrase in verse was the age of crudities in prose

text: M. Gillenormand's Christian names: Luc (Luke) and Esprit, which in French means both 'spirit' and 'wit'. His godfather chose them as a prophecy that he would be clever; Hugo calls them 'significant'.
quote: these two significant names: Luc-Esprit

term: The Duc de Nivernais and the blue ribbon
text: Louis-Jules Mancini-Mazarini, Duc de Nivernais (1716–1798), diplomat, minor poet and the model of a polished grand seigneur, who handed out school prizes in his duchy around Nevers. The blue ribbon was the sash of the Order of the Holy Spirit, the highest order of the French monarchy. M. Gillenormand has treasured his prize-giving for seventy years.
quote: he had been crowned by the hand of the Duc de Nivernais

text: A fashionable eighteenth-century nostrum, sold as 'General Lamotte's drops' and the 'yellow tincture' of the Russian chancellor Bestuzhev, and supposed to cure venereal disease ('the catastrophes of love'). At a louis the half-ounce it was a luxury remedy. Hugo deflates it: it was iron chloride.
quote: the elixir of gold, from Bestucheff

text: A pun on 1793, the year of the Terror, when the Revolution guillotined the king and thousands of suspects. M. Gillenormand, who boasts of having slipped through it, means he hopes to reach the age of ninety-three without living through another such year.
quote: “I hope that I shall not see ninety-three twice.”

text: During the Revolution the lands of the Church and of émigré nobles were confiscated as biens nationaux and sold off. M. Gillenormand has seen inherited estates vanish that way, which is one reason he prefers to sink his capital in an annuity that dies with him.
quote: become “national property;”

term: Three percents and the Great Book
text: The 'consolidated three percent' was French government stock paying three per cent a year, recorded in the Grand Livre de la Dette Publique (the Great Book of the Public Debt). Its value rose and fell with every change of regime, and in 1797 the Directory wrote off two-thirds of the debt at a stroke: hence the old man's distrust.
quote: he had been present at the avatars of consolidated three percents

text: The narrow Paris street where the Scottish financier John Law ran his Mississippi Company bank in 1719–20, scene of a wild speculative frenzy and then a crash that ruined thousands. 'That's the Rue Quincampoix!' means 'that's a swindle, paper wealth'.
quote: “All that’s the Rue Quincampois!”

text: Old-regime masters often called a servant not by his own name but by his province of origin (Picard, Poitevin, Basque) or gave every maid the same name, as English houses called footmen 'James'. M. Gillenormand keeps the habit: every man is named for his province and every woman is 'Nicolette', even if he must raise her wages to make it stick.
quote: When a servant entered his establishment, M. Gillenormand re-baptized him.

text: 'Blue ribbon': a first-class cook. The phrase borrowed the name of the royal Order of the Holy Spirit, whose blue sash was the highest honour of the old monarchy. Thirty francs a month was a good wage for a cook, and fifty a very generous one.
quote: a cordon bleu, of the lofty race of porters

text: Latin from Virgil's Fourth Eclogue: 'let the woods be worthy of a consul'. M. Gillenormand twists it into a complaint that if he must be robbed 'as though in a forest', the robbery should at least be worthy of a man of his standing.
quote: Silvae sint consule dignae!

term: The Duc d'Angoulême, bastard of Charles IX
text: Charles de Valois (1573–1650), the illegitimate son of King Charles IX, who in his old age married a girl of about twenty and had children by her. Not to be confused with the Restoration Duc d'Angoulême. M. Gillenormand reels off such precedents to show he is quite flattered that a baby is laid at his door at eighty-four.
quote: M. le Duc d’Angoulême, the bastard of his Majesty Charles IX

text: What M. Gillenormand agrees to pay Magnon for the keep of the two boys she says are his: nearly a thousand francs a year, about two years of a labourer's wages. It is a generous sum for a man who calls himself ruined.
quote: promising to pay eighty francs a month for their maintenance

text: Copper coins withdrawn from circulation and no longer legal tender, worthless in a shop. The miserly priest-brother gave them as alms, keeping the form of charity while giving nothing, 'going to hell by way of paradise'.
quote: he never gave them anything except bad or demonetized sous

text: The left-bank quarter of great noble mansions round the Rue de Grenelle and Saint-Sulpice, home of the old aristocracy after the Revolution and the heart of ultra-royalist society under the Restoration. The Rue Servandoni, where M. Gillenormand first lived, runs beside the church of Saint-Sulpice.
quote: lived in the Faubourg Saint Germain, Rue Servandoni, near Saint-Sulpice

text: Oreilles de chien: long locks of hair hanging over the ears on either side of the face, a style of the Directory dandies of the 1790s. M. Gillenormand keeps it, like his clothes, from the last fashion he followed.
quote: always dressed in “dog’s ears.”

text: Eighteenth-century society dined early in the afternoon and paid and received calls in the evening by candlelight; the daytime was for business and for people who worked. M. Gillenormand's rule (dinner at five, door open after) is a deliberately antique habit.
quote: never to receive anyone whatever except in the evening

text: The wife of a prefect, the government's chief official in a département, who presided over official receptions and balls in the provincial capital. In French a wife took her husband's title as a courtesy, so to marry a prefect was to become 'Madame la Préfète'.
quote: to be “Madame la Préfète,”

text: Light cavalry armed with lances, a fashionable arm revived in the French army after Napoleon's Polish lancers. An officer of Lancers had a dashing uniform and a reputation to match.
quote: an officer of the Lancers, her grand nephew, named Théodule

term: Society of the Virgin; the sacred heart
text: Under the Restoration, pious lay associations ('congregations') flourished under Jesuit guidance, and the devotions to the Sacred Heart of Jesus and the Precious Blood were their badges. Liberals mocked them as political as well as religious: piety went with ultra-royalism. Mademoiselle Gillenormand practises the full set.
quote: She belonged to the society of the Virgin

text: The ornate eighteenth-century style of church decoration favoured by the Jesuits: gilded wooden rays, marble clouds and cherubs. Hugo, a lover of Gothic, uses it as a sign of showy, shallow devotion.
quote: before a rococo-Jesuit altar

text: Latin prayers: 'Lamb of God', said at mass before communion, and 'Hail Mary'. Mademoiselle Vaubois knows these and how to make jam, and nothing else.
quote: Beyond the Agnus Dei and Ave Maria

text: Louis de Bonald (1754–1840), the leading philosopher of the counter-revolution, who argued that society rests on God, the king and the father, and who led the ultra-royalists in the Chamber after 1815. To hold one's own against Bonald was a feat in a royalist salon.
quote: against M. de Bonald

text: Under the Restoration, the 'ultras' wanted the old monarchy back whole and thought even Louis XVIII, with his constitutional Charter and moderate ministers, a crypto-Jacobin. They pinned their hopes on the king's brother, the Comte d'Artois. Madame de T.'s salon is a small, poor, fierce outpost of that party.
quote: the Jacobinism of Louis XVIII

text: In royalist street songs of 1814–15 Napoleon was mocked as 'Nicolas', a name for a simpleton. The fédérés were the volunteer workers' battalions raised in Paris during the Hundred Days to defend the Emperor; the duchesses' song tells them to tuck their shirt-tails in, a jeer at the white flag of surrender.
quote: Napoleon was called “Nicolas,”

text: The moderate cabinet of 1818–19 under General Dessolles included Decazes, Louis XVIII's liberal-leaning favourite, and De Serre. The royalist couplet says that to steady the throne one must change 'sol, serre and case', the soil, greenhouse and hut, which sound like the ministers' names. This is the salon's idea of a deadly epigram.
quote: Il faut changer de sol, et de serre et de case.

text: 'It'll be fine': the revolutionary song of 1790 whose refrain called for aristocrats to be strung up 'à la lanterne', from the street lamp-posts. The royalists sing it with Bonapartists in place of aristocrats. Hugo's comment: songs, like the guillotine, cut any head.
quote: Les Bonapartistes à la lanterne!

text: The sensational murder of Antoine Fualdès, a former magistrate, in Rodez in 1817 (Hugo writes 1816); Bastide and Jausion were tried and executed for it. Because Fualdès had served the Empire, the royalist salons sided with the accused.
quote: In the Fualdès affair

term: Lamothe-Valois and the affair of the necklace
text: In 1785 the adventuress Jeanne de La Motte-Valois, who claimed descent from the Valois kings, tricked Cardinal de Rohan into buying a fabulous diamond necklace supposedly for Marie-Antoinette, then had it broken up and sold. The scandal stained the queen's name on the eve of the Revolution. Her husband, the Comte de La Motte, escaped with the diamonds; in Madame de T.'s salon he is received with respect.
quote: “Do you know? That is the Lamothe of the affair of the necklace.”

text: Examples of the old nobility's indifference to scandal: Marigny was the brother of Madame de Pompadour, Louis XV's mistress; Jean du Barry was the pimp who launched Jeanne Bécu ('the Vaubernier') as the future Madame du Barry; the Prince de Guémenée went spectacularly bankrupt in 1782. All were welcome in the best houses. Mercury was the god of thieves.
quote: Marigny, the brother of the Pompadour, had his entry with M. le Prince de Soubise

text: The incognito under which King Frederick William III of Prussia visited Paris after the allies restored Louis XVIII. Louis treated him like a provincial marquis, as if the house of Bourbon still outranked every other crown, which M. Gillenormand applauds.
quote: under the name of the Count de Ruppin

text: A pun: a newspaper editor 'suspendu' (suspended) should simply be 'pendu', hanged. The Courrier Français was a leading liberal paper of the Restoration, frequently prosecuted.
quote: “Sus is superfluous,” observed M. Gillenormand.

text: The Latin hymn of thanksgiving ('We praise thee, O God') sung at state services for victories and royal anniversaries. Every year the Restoration celebrated the return of the Bourbons with one, and Talleyrand, who had served every regime, was naturally there.
quote: At the Te Deum on the anniversary of the return of the Bourbons

text: After Waterloo the remains of Napoleon's army withdrew behind the Loire and were disbanded there in the autumn of 1815. Royalists called its officers 'the brigands of the Loire', and many were put on half-pay and watched by the police. In the Gillenormand household it is the name for the boy's father.
quote: he had for a father “a brigand of the Loire.”

text: A small Norman town on the Seine about seventy kilometres down-river from Paris, on the road to Rouen, with an old stone bridge and walled gardens running down to the water. Far enough from the capital for an officer under surveillance, close enough to slip into Paris.
quote: the little town of Vernon

text: The Restoration put thousands of Napoleon's officers on demi-solde, half pay without duties, and sent the suspect ones to live in an assigned town under police watch. The 'demi-soldes', bitter and poor, were a byword for Bonapartist discontent.
quote: The Restoration had placed him on half-pay, then had sent him into residence

term: Ranks granted in the Hundred Days
text: Louis XVIII treated everything Napoleon did between his return from Elba and Waterloo as void, so promotions and titles given in those months were not recognised. A colonel and baron made on the field of Waterloo became officially a chef d'escadron again, and his Legion of Honour officer's rosette 'illegal'.
quote: did not recognize his quality as an officer of the Legion of Honor, nor his grade of colonel, nor his title of baron

text: Hugo's list runs through the whole revolutionary and Napoleonic saga: the Rhine campaigns of 1792–93, Italy and Lodi (1796), Novi (1799), Ulm and Austerlitz (1805), Eylau and Friedland (1807), Moscow and the Berezina (1812), Leipzig (1813), the defence of France (1814), Elba and Waterloo. A soldier who saw all of these had lived the Empire from end to end.
quote: Pontmercy fought at Spire, at Worms, at Neustadt

text: Victor Hugo's uncle, who held the cemetery at Eylau with a single company through the snowstorm battle of February 1807. Hugo's father was also a Napoleonic general, and this personal aside is a sign of how close the Empire's legend was to his own family.
quote: the heroic Captain Louis Hugo, the uncle of the author of this book

text: Heavy cavalry wearing steel breastplates (cuirasses) and helmets, used for massed charges. At Waterloo they made the great charges against the British squares. A 'chief of squadron' commanded a squadron of a cavalry regiment.
quote: he was chief of a squadron of cuirassiers

text: The British governor of Saint Helena, Napoleon's jailer from 1816 to his death in 1821. He addressed him only as 'General Bonaparte', refusing the imperial title, and Napoleon sent such letters back unopened.
quote: the missives of Sir Hudson Lowe addressed to “General Bonaparte.”

text: An image from Roman history: Carthaginian captives in Rome who refused to salute a Roman consul, keeping the pride of Hannibal, their general. Flaminius was in fact the consul Hannibal destroyed at Lake Trasimene.
quote: there were at Rome Carthaginian prisoners who refused to salute Flaminius

text: Étienne Soulange-Bodin (1774–1846), a former soldier who became one of France's great horticulturists and founded the Paris horticultural society. Hugo says the colonel anticipated his beds of heath-mould for rare American and Chinese shrubs.
quote: he had forestalled Soulange Bodin

text: A churchwarden: a layman of the parish who sat on the council (the fabrique) managing a church's property and accounts, with a reserved pew. Saint-Sulpice was the great church of the Faubourg Saint-Germain.
quote: That worthy priest was the brother of a warden of Saint-Sulpice

text: 23 April, the feast of Saint George. In Catholic France a person celebrated the feast of his patron saint, his 'name-day', more than his birthday, so the boy's letters went on New Year's Day and on the name-day of his father, Georges.
quote: on the first of January and on St. George’s day

text: Real old noble family names that happen to sound biblical: Mathan is a priest of Baal in the Book of Kings, Noé is Noah, Lévis was pronounced like Levi, and Cambis like Cambyses, the Persian king. To a small boy learning the Old Testament by heart, the old ladies round the fire become patriarchs and magi.
quote: some very noble ladies named Mathan, Noé, Lévis—which was pronounced Lévi—Cambis, pronounced Cambyse

text: Marie-Caroline, Duchesse de Berry, wife of the king's nephew the Duc de Berry, whose assassination in 1820 left her the mother of the posthumous Bourbon heir. Her household was a centre of ultra-royalist hopes.
quote: private secretary to Madame de Berry

text: Under the Revolution a 'refractory' priest was one who refused the oath to the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (1790), and a refractory soldier one who refused to serve the Republic. Both were hunted. The chevalier's story of being chained at Toulon with an old bishop and made to carry away the guillotined is a typical salon horror tale.
quote: he had been put in the galleys as refractory and chained with an octogenarian, the Bishop of Mirepoix

text: Jean-Paul Marat was the journalist of the Terror who called for heads in his paper 'L'Ami du peuple' until Charlotte Corday stabbed him in 1793. Trestaillon was the nickname of Jacques Dupont, leader of royalist gangs that murdered Protestants and Bonapartists around Nîmes in the White Terror of 1815. The salon curses one and cheers the other.
quote: by dint of cursing Marat, they applauded Trestaillon

text: The Chamber of Deputies elected in August 1815 was so ultra-royalist that Louis XVIII called it la Chambre introuvable, the 'chamber one could never have hoped to find'. Hugo's deputies at the whist table are members of it.
quote: Some deputies of the undiscoverable variety played their whist there

text: Denis Frayssinous (1765–1841), a famous preacher who became Grand Master of the University and Minister of Ecclesiastical Affairs under Charles X, and a count, bishop and peer. Hugo shows him earlier, in a cassock with buttons missing.
quote: the Abbé Frayssinous, who was not, as yet, either count, or bishop, or minister, or peer

text: Short for in partibus infidelium, 'in the lands of the unbelievers': a bishop given the title of an ancient see now in Muslim territory (here Carystus in Greece), so that he has the rank without a diocese. Such titles went to papal diplomats and assistants like the cardinal's conclavist.
quote: Bishop in partibus of Caryste

text: A member of the Académie française, which has forty seats held for life. In those years it met in the Institut building on the Quai Conti; on Tuesdays passers-by could watch the academicians through the glass door.
quote: and one of the Forty

text: Members of the hereditary upper house created by Louis XVIII's Charter of 1814, on the English model of the House of Lords. The Duc de Valentinois, also reigning Prince of Monaco, thought being a French peer so much grander that he described cardinals as 'peers of France of Rome'.
quote: accentuated by five peers of France

text: 'Le Père Duchesne' was the foul-mouthed revolutionary newspaper of Jacques Hébert in the 1790s, written in the voice of a swearing stove-maker. Even Chateaubriand, the great royalist writer, would have shocked this salon as much as Hébert.
quote: Chateaubriand, had he entered there, would have produced the effect of Père Duchêne.

text: A fagot is a bundle of sticks, the fuel for burning heretics at the stake; to 'smell of the fagot' meant to be suspected of heresy. Hugo turns it round: the aristocratic quarter still smells of the stake, of persecution.
quote: The Faubourg Saint-Germain reeks of the fagot even now.

term: Madame la Générale, Madame la Colonelle
text: The old custom of giving a wife her husband's military rank as a title. By the 1820s it sounded provincial to outsiders, but in this salon it was simply the manners of the old court surviving.
quote: A woman was called Madame la Générale.

text: Napoleon had been addressed as 'Your Majesty', so the purest royalists stopped using the phrase for Louis XVIII and spoke to him in the third person as 'the King'. For them the 'usurper' was Bonaparte.
quote: the designation of “Your Majesty” having been “soiled by the usurper.”

term: Coblentz and the twenty-fifth year of the reign
text: Coblenz on the Rhine was where the émigré princes gathered their army in 1791–92. Louis XVIII dated his reign from 1795, the death of his young nephew Louis XVII in prison, so his Charter of 1814 was given 'in the nineteenth year of our reign', as though the Republic and the Empire had never happened. Hugo mocks the émigrés for counting the same way.
quote: They declared that the time which had elapsed since Coblentz had not existed.

text: Methuselah is the man in Genesis who lived 969 years; Epimenides the Cretan sage said to have slept for fifty-seven years in a cave. One very old man brings the news to another who has slept through it all: Hugo's picture of the salon.
quote: Methuselah bestowed information on Epimenides

text: Short for ultra-royaliste: those who wanted to be more royalist than the king, rejecting the Charter and every compromise with the Revolution. Hugo defines the word as 'so strongly for, as to be against' and says the ultra spirit marks the years 1814–1820.
quote: What did they do in Madame de T.’s salon? They were ultra.

text: Joseph de Villèle (1773–1854), the shrewd, businesslike leader of the royalist right who ran the government from 1821 to 1828. Hugo marks his arrival as the end of the first, romantic phase of the Restoration.
quote: with the advent of M. de Villèle, the practical man of the Right

text: Fontenoy (1745) was a celebrated victory of Louis XV's army, Marengo (1800) one of Bonaparte's. The old nobility sneered at the Empire's soldiers and the Empire's soldiers sneered back; each side despised the other's swords.
quote: the sword of Fontenoy was laughable and nothing but a scrap of rusty iron; the sword of Marengo was odious and was only a sabre

text: The scheming, quick-witted valet of Molière's comedy 'Les Fourberies de Scapin' (1671). To call Bonaparte Scapin was to reduce the conqueror of Europe to a clever lackey.
quote: There was someone who called Bonaparte Scapin.

text: Royalist journalists and pamphleteers of the early Restoration, much read in their own circle and soon forgotten. Martainville edited the ultra paper 'Le Drapeau blanc'. That he 'had more wit than Voltaire' is Hugo's irony.
quote: when M. Martainville had more wit than Voltaire

term: The Corsican Ogre; M. le Marquis de Bonaparte
text: Royalist propaganda painted Napoleon as an ogre from Corsica who devoured France's young men. A Jesuit school textbook by Father Loriquet was popularly believed to have called him 'the Marquis de Bonaparte, lieutenant-general of the King's armies', erasing the Empire altogether; Hugo cites it as a 'concession' to the times.
quote: Napoleon was to them thoroughly the Corsican Ogre

text: The doctrinaires were a small group of liberal royalists (Royer-Collard and Guizot the best known) who wanted a constitutional monarchy reconciling the Bourbons with the gains of the Revolution. Hugo lets them speak at length: their plea to 'love the whole of France', old and new, is close to his own.
quote: Beginning with 1818, doctrinarians began to spring up in them

term: The 5th of September and the N's of the bridge of Jéna
text: On 5 September 1816 Louis XVIII dissolved the ultra 'Chambre introuvable', a defeat for the old nobility; in July 1815 it had been the Empire's people who were purged. M. de Vaublanc, an ultra minister, had Napoleon's N's chiselled off the Pont d'Iéna. Bouvines (1214) was a great victory of the medieval French crown.
quote: We scoff at M. de Vaublanc for erasing the N’s from the bridge of Jéna!

text: A Catholic lay society under Jesuit direction, founded under the Empire and believed by liberals to be the hidden power behind the Restoration's later years, placing its members in office. 'Congregation' became shorthand for clerical influence in politics.
quote: congregation characterized the second

text: Hugo's mother, Sophie Trébuchet, was a royalist from the Vendée region, and he himself was a fervent young royalist poet under the Restoration. His affectionate sketch of a world he has since rejected is partly a family memory.
quote: Souvenirs both respectful and affectionate, for they touch his mother

term: Coaches from the Cour des Fontaines
text: Before railways, coaches for Normandy left from coaching yards in central Paris, such as the Cour des Fontaines by the Palais-Royal and the Rue du Bouloi nearby. A day coach took twelve hours to Vernon; a night diligence to Rouen would have got Marius there by morning, and nobody looked into it.
quote: there is a coach which leaves the Cour des Fontaines at six o’clock

text: Le sabreur: a soldier good only at swinging a sabre, a sneer at Napoleon's officers as brutes without breeding. M. Gillenormand uses it 'on his amiable days', when he is not saying 'brigand'.
quote: “the slasher,” as M. Gillenormand called him on his amiable days

text: A nineteenth-century catch-all for an illness with high fever and delirium: meningitis, encephalitis, or typhoid in its worst stage. It killed quickly, which is why the colonel wrote at once.
quote: The colonel had been attacked by brain fever three days previously.

text: Napoleon created a new nobility from 1808, with titles (count, baron, chevalier) given for service and transmissible to sons. A barony conferred on the field was the soldier's dream. The Restoration let most imperial titles stand but not those of the Hundred Days, so the colonel's title was disputed.
quote: The Emperor made me a Baron on the battlefield of Waterloo.

text: A band of black crape round the hat was the outward sign of a man in mourning for a close relative. It is the smallest gesture custom required, and 'that was all'.
quote: Marius wore crape on his hat. That was all.

text: French churches had no fixed pews; worshippers hired straw or velvet chairs from a chair-woman at each service, and regulars and officials had their own chairs with their names on the back. A churchwarden also had a right to a stall. Utrecht velvet was a thick, stamped upholstery velvet.
quote: upon a chair of Utrecht velvet, on the back of which was inscribed this name: “Monsieur Mabeuf, warden.”

text: 'My God': a mild, everyday French exclamation, no stronger than 'good heavens'. Hapgood often leaves it in French.
quote: Mon Dieu! a man is not a monster because he was at Waterloo

text: Le Moniteur universel, founded in 1789, the official newspaper of every French government from the Revolution on, printing laws, debates, decrees and army bulletins. Its back files are the raw record of the age, which is why Marius goes to it first.
quote: asked for the files of the Moniteur

text: Las Cases's record of Napoleon's conversations in exile on Saint Helena, published in 1823. It shaped the legend of the Emperor as a liberal hero martyred by the kings, and was the best-seller that made a generation of young men Bonapartists.
quote: the Memorial de Sainte-Hélène

text: Napoleon's official dispatches from the field, written or dictated by himself, published in the Moniteur and read aloud across France. Vivid and self-glorifying, they named regiments and officers who had distinguished themselves; Hugo calls them 'heroic strophes'.
quote: the bulletins of the grand army

text: Great figures of the Revolution: Mirabeau, the thunderous orator of 1789; Vergniaud, leader of the Girondins, guillotined in 1793; Saint-Just, Robespierre's young ally, guillotined with him in 1794. Hugo lists them with Robespierre, Desmoulins and Danton as the 'stars' Marius discovers.
quote: Mirabeau, Vergniaud, Saint-Just, Robespierre, Camille, Desmoulins, Danton

text: One of the generals Marius visits. The initial is a private nod: Hugo's own father, Léopold Hugo, was a Napoleonic general and count.
quote: among others, Comte H.

text: The slanders royalist pamphlets spread about Bonaparte: incest with his sisters, lessons in posing from the actor Talma, and the poisoning of his own plague-stricken soldiers at Jaffa during the Syrian campaign of 1799. Marius had swallowed them all as a boy.
quote: the monster who was the lover of his own sisters—the actor who took lessons of Talma—the poisoner of Jaffa

text: The twelve-man executive of the Revolutionary government in 1793–94, dominated by Robespierre, which ran the war and the Terror. That Marius puts it in a line of nation-builders from Charlemagne and Louis XI to Richelieu and Louis XIV shows how far he has swung.
quote: of Louis XIV, and of the Committee of Public Safety

text: La Grande Nation: the name revolutionary and Napoleonic France gave itself as the liberator and leader of Europe. To Marius, Napoleon is the man who made the other nations say it.
quote: who had forced all nations to say: “The great nation!”

text: A supporter of the exiled Stuart kings of Britain after 1688; by extension, a diehard legitimist loyal to a deposed dynasty. It is not the same as Jacobin, the radical revolutionary. Marius sheds both his royalism and this die-hard loyalty to the old line.
quote: the aristocrat, the Jacobite and the Royalist

text: Engraved cards left at the door or with the porter when calling on someone, the basic tool of social life. The Quai des Orfèvres, the goldsmiths' quay on the Île de la Cité, was where engravers worked. A hundred cards for 'Le Baron Marius Pontmercy', claiming his father's disputed title, and no one to leave them with.
quote: he went to an engraver on the Quai des Orfévres and ordered a hundred cards

text: Géronte is the stock foolish old father of French comedy (in Molière's 'Scapin' among others); Werther is the melancholy young hero of Goethe's 'The Sorrows of Young Werther' (1774). Hugo uses the pair for a frivolous grandfather and a brooding grandson.
quote: The gayety of Géronte shocks and exasperates the melancholy of Werther.

text: The largest planet, bright in the night sky. Hugo's figure is generous: Jupiter's volume is about 1,300 times the Earth's. The cosmic scale sets up Marius's midnight cry from the window.
quote: one beholds Jupiter, which is twelve hundred times larger than the earth

text: The compartments of a French diligence, or stage-coach. The coupé was the closed front compartment with a window onto the road, the dearest seats; the impériale was the bench on the roof under a hood, the cheapest. The officer rides inside in comfort; the student rides on top.
quote: He in the imperial, I in the coupé.

text: The louis was the gold coin worth twenty francs, so the aunt's present is two hundred francs: several months' pay for a junior officer's pocket, and plenty to make Théodule obliging.
quote: And she put ten louis into his hand.

text: From Spanish dueña: an older woman employed to chaperone a young lady and keep watch on her suitors. A dashing lancer sent to spy on a young man's love affair feels he has been demoted to a governess.
quote: “Here I am a duenna.”

text: Louis-Dominique Cartouche, the most famous Paris highwayman and gang leader of the early eighteenth century, broken on the wheel in 1721 and turned into a folk hero. The grimace of 'Cartouche praised for his probity' is a rogue being complimented on his honesty.
quote: The lancer made the pleased grimace of Cartouche when praised for his probity.

text: The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth set by Hera to watch Io, whose eyes never all closed at once until Hermes lulled him to sleep. The spy who snores all night is a comic Argus.
quote: Argus snored all night long.

text: Fillette, 'little girl', used by men of M. Gillenormand's and Théodule's kind for a working girl taken as a mistress. The aunt is convinced because she hears her father's very word and tone in the lieutenant's mouth.
quote: at that word fillette

text: Théodule is a pious old saint's name; Alfred was the fashionable romantic name of the 1820s and 30s (Alfred de Musset, Alfred de Vigny). The lieutenant would rather be in fashion than in the calendar of saints.
quote: “I would rather be called Alfred,” said the officer.

text: Coaches changed horses every few leagues at post-houses, the 'relays'; the postilion rode one of the leading horses to guide the team. Villagers sold flowers and food to passengers during the change.
quote: “Vernon! relay of Vernon! Travellers for Vernon!”

text: Paris had floating bath-houses moored on the Seine, with enclosed pools where men swam and bathed; most homes had no bathroom. After two nights on a coach roof, Marius goes for an hour's swim.
quote: by an hour at the swimming-school

text: A rough, grainy leather made from the skin of a horse or shark, often dyed black or green and used for small cases. The little black case on a ribbon looks to M. Gillenormand like a locket portrait of a mistress.
quote: a case of black shagreen, resembling a medallion portrait

text: French, 'sweet note': a love letter. 'From the same to the same' is M. Gillenormand's knowing joke that a man keeps his lady's letters next to her picture.
quote: “From the same to the same,” said M. Gillenormand, bursting with laughter. “I know what it is. A billet-doux.”

text: The red Phrygian cap, the bonnet rouge, was the emblem of the radical sans-culottes of 1792–94 and of liberty in general. To an old royalist, 'redcap' means a Terrorist.
quote: assassins, redcaps, thieves!

text: Royalists pointedly used the Italian spelling of Napoleon's family name, Buonaparte, and gave it an Italian sound, to stress that he was a Corsican foreigner, not a French sovereign. M. Gillenormand spells it out syllable by syllable for emphasis.
quote: All who served B-u-o-naparté were brigands!

text: Charles-Ferdinand, Duc de Berry (1778–1820), the king's nephew and the hope of the dynasty, stabbed outside the Opéra in 1820 by a Bonapartist workman, Louvel. His bust on a royalist mantelpiece was a shrine; M. Gillenormand bows to it as if apologising for what has just been said.
quote: a bust of M. le Duc de Berry

term: 'Louis XVIII had been dead for four years'
text: Louis XVIII died in September 1824 and was succeeded by his brother, Charles X, so the scene is in 1828. Marius's insult is political rather than accurate.
quote: Louis XVIII had been dead for four years; but it was all the same to him.

text: The pistole was an old name for a gold coin worth about ten livres, still used in speech by people of M. Gillenormand's age. Sixty pistoles every six months is about six hundred francs, so 1,200 francs a year: a modest student allowance, sent with a curse.
quote: You will send sixty pistoles every six months to that blood-drinker

text: A French father said tu ('thou') to his children. Calling his daughter vous, the formal 'you', for three months is M. Gillenormand's way of keeping his anger cold: an icy, polite distance.
quote: he continued to address his daughter as “you” instead of “thou” for the next three months

text: A fiacre, the Paris cab, could be hired by the trip or by the hour. Marius, with thirty francs and no plan, takes one by the hour and drives at random.
quote: He had entered a hackney-coach, had engaged it by the hour

text: The left-bank district round the Sorbonne, the law and medical schools and the Panthéon, home of students, cheap lodgings, cafés and printing shops, so called because Latin was once the language of its schools. It is the natural refuge for a penniless law student.
quote: towards the Latin quarter

text: The Tugendbund ('League of Virtue') was a Prussian patriotic society of 1808 aimed at throwing off Napoleon; the Carbonari ('charcoal-burners') were the Italian secret society that organised risings against Austrian and Bourbon rule from about 1815, with a French offshoot, the Charbonnerie, in the early 1820s. Hugo's point is that France had nothing so large, only small circles.
quote: like the German tugendbund and Italian Carbonarism

text: A republican secret society of Provence; the name is Provençal for a gourd. Hugo places its beginnings at Aix in these years. He mentions it alongside the Paris group as one of several shoots of the same underground growth.
quote: The Cougourde was being outlined at Aix

text: A pun: in French the letters A, B, C are pronounced 'ah-bay-say', the same sound as abaissé, 'brought low', 'debased'. The name passes for a society to teach children their letters while meaning 'Friends of the downtrodden'. Hugo's examples show that puns have made history before.
quote: They declared themselves the Friends of the A.B.C.—the Abaissé—the debased—that is to say, the people.

term: Castratus ad castra; Barbari et Barberini; Tu es Petrus
text: Three famous puns. Narses, the Byzantine general, was a eunuch, so 'the castrated man to the camp'; Pasquino's Roman jibe 'what the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did' mocked Pope Urban VIII's family for stripping the Pantheon's bronze; and Christ's 'Thou art Peter (Petrus), and upon this rock (petram) I will build my church' (Matthew 16:18) is the pun on which the papacy rests.
quote: witness the Castratus ad castra, which made a general of the army of Narses

text: The two haunts of the group. The Café Musain was a small café near the Panthéon with a back room reached by a long corridor and a private stair onto the Rue des Grès; Corinthe was a wine-shop near the old fish-market of Les Halles on the right bank. One is close to the students, the other to the workmen.
quote: in a little café in the Rue Saint-Michel called the Café Musain, now torn down

term: A map of France under the Republic
text: A map showing the départements of the Republic, or the frontiers of 1792–1799, instead of the kingdom: under the Restoration, hanging one was a quiet political statement, enough to draw a police spy's eye.
quote: An old map of France under the Republic was nailed to the wall

text: The beautiful youth loved by the Emperor Hadrian, drowned in the Nile in AD 130 and deified; his statues became the classic type of young male beauty. A 'savage Antinous' is beauty with a fierce edge.
quote: He was a savage Antinous.

text: Gaius Gracchus, the Roman tribune who championed land reform for the poor, made his last stand with his followers on the Aventine hill in 121 BC and died there. Saint-Just was the youngest and most uncompromising of the Jacobins in the Convention.
quote: On Mount Aventine, he would have been Gracchus; in the Convention, he would have been Saint-Just.

text: The two Athenians who in 514 BC killed the tyrant's brother Hipparchus, hiding their daggers in myrtle branches at a festival, and were honoured as liberators. Evadne stands for any beautiful woman. To Enjolras, as to them, flowers are good only to hide a sword.
quote: he, like Harmodius, thought flowers good for nothing except to conceal the sword

term: The cherub of Ezekiel and the Cherubino of Beaumarchais
text: The cherubim in Ezekiel's vision are terrible, four-faced, winged beings of fire. Chérubin is the amorous teenage page of Beaumarchais's 'Marriage of Figaro', in love with every woman. A girl who took Enjolras for the second would meet the first.
quote: not to confound the mighty cherub of Ezekiel with the gallant Cherubino of Beaumarchais

text: The Marquis de Condorcet (1743–1794), mathematician and philosopher of the Revolution, who believed in the indefinite progress of humanity through reason and education, and wrote his 'Sketch' of that progress while hiding from the Terror. He died in prison. Robespierre is the model for Enjolras, Condorcet for Combeferre.
quote: The first attached himself to Robespierre; the second confined himself to Condorcet.

text: Two Latin words for 'man': homo, the human being, and vir, the male, the man of courage (the root of 'virile' and 'virtue'). Combeferre is the humane one, Enjolras the virile one.
quote: Homo and vir, that was the exact effect of their different shades.

text: Leading Paris scientists of the 1820s whose public lectures drew students: François Arago, the physicist and astronomer who worked on the polarization of light, and Étienne Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire, the naturalist of the Jardin des Plantes who argued for a unity of plan across animal bodies. Combeferre follows them both.
quote: learned the polarization of light from Arago

text: The two founders of French socialism. Henri de Saint-Simon (1760–1825) wanted society run by industrialists and scientists for the good of the poorest; Charles Fourier (1772–1837) planned ideal communities, 'phalansteries', where work would be made attractive. Comparing them was what a serious young reformer did in 1828.
quote: compared Saint-Simon with Fourier

text: Followers of Mesmer who studied 'animal magnetism' and the trance state called magnetic sleep, an early form of hypnotism. Combeferre reads them with an open mind: he affirms nothing and denies nothing.
quote: studied Puységur and Deleuze

text: The École Polytechnique, founded in 1794 on the Montagne Sainte-Geneviève, France's elite school of engineering and science, run on military lines. Its students had a strong republican tradition.
quote: a graduate of the Polytechnic

text: Hugo lists inventions that were still dreams in 1828 and realities when he wrote in the 1860s: railways, anaesthesia for surgery (ether, 1846), photography (images fixed in the camera obscura, 1839), the electric telegraph. Only the steerable balloon was still to come.
quote: railroads, the suppression of suffering in chirurgical operations, the fixing of images in the dark chamber, the electric telegraph, the steering of balloons

text: The medieval spelling of Jean. Hugo's own 'Notre-Dame de Paris' (1831) had helped launch the Romantic craze for the Middle Ages, and some young men took to old-fashioned spellings of their names. Prouvaire's 'Jehan' marks him as a poet of that school.
quote: His name was Jehan

text: The finest French poet of the late eighteenth century, guillotined in July 1794, two days before the fall of Robespierre. Hugo calls him 'a royal head', royal in poetry; Prouvaire holds his death against the Revolution.
quote: that of André Chénier

text: Théodore Agrippa d'Aubigné (1552–1630), Protestant soldier and poet whose epic 'Les Tragiques' rages against the persecution of the Huguenots. Preferring Corneille's grandeur to Racine's refinement, and d'Aubigné's fury to both, marks Prouvaire's taste for the 'immense'.
quote: he preferred Corneille to Racine, and Agrippa d’Aubigné to Corneille

term: Fan-maker at three francs a day
text: Fan-making was a skilled Paris craft (painting and mounting the leaves of fans). Three francs a day was a decent wage for a workman, enough to live on alone but not to buy books, which Feuilly does anyway.
quote: Feuilly was a workingman, a fan-maker, orphaned both of father and mother, who earned with difficulty three francs a day

text: In 1772 Russia, Prussia and Austria each seized a slice of Poland; two more partitions in 1793 and 1795 wiped it off the map. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 confirmed most of it, putting Warsaw under the Tsar. To Feuilly this 'three-sided crime' is the pattern for every later suppression of a nation.
quote: Above all things, the great violence of 1772 aroused him.

text: Latin legal phrase, 'let it not be altered', stamped on a document to certify it as the fixed, authentic text. Every despot since, says Feuilly, has signed a copy of the partition of Poland without changing a word.
quote: ne variatur

text: The little 'de' before a surname (de Courfeyrac, de Lafayette), widely taken as a sign of nobility, though it proves nothing. Under the Restoration liberal gentlemen dropped it to show their politics: Lafayette, Benjamin Constant. La Minerve was the leading liberal review of 1818–1820.
quote: But the bourgeois of the epoch of la Minerve estimated so highly that poor de, that they thought themselves bound to abdicate it.

text: 'The devil's beauty': the bloom of youth, attractive whatever the features, that fades with age. Hugo applies it to the mind: Courfeyrac's sparkle is the same student wit as Tholomyès's, passed down the generations.
quote: the beauté du diable of the mind

text: From Lucretius: 'and like runners they pass on the torch of life'. The generations of students hand on the same jokes and the same style of wit as relay runners hand on a torch.
quote: quasi cursores

text: Nicolas Lallemand, a law student, was shot by a soldier of the royal guard during demonstrations over a new electoral law in June 1820 (Hugo writes 1822); his funeral turned into a mass liberal protest broken up by troops. It was the first time Restoration students fought in the streets.
quote: the burial of young Lallemand

term: The square cap in the nightstand
text: The square cap (bonnet carré) was the cap of a lawyer or judge; a nightstand was the bedside cupboard that held the chamber pot. Bahorel's mock coat of arms puts the one in the other: that is his opinion of the law.
quote: for his armorial bearings a nightstand in which was visible a square cap

text: A loose, short overcoat that became the fashion in the 1830s and 40s. Hugo's aside 'the paletot had not yet been invented' dates the scene: in 1828 a student still buttoned up a fitted frock-coat.
quote: the paletot had not yet been invented

text: Antoine de Béziade, Comte (later Duc) d'Avaray, the friend who smuggled the future Louis XVIII out of Paris in a cab in June 1791, when Louis XVI's own flight failed at Varennes. The king rewarded him lavishly; Hugo says it was for helping him into a hackney-coach.
quote: The Marquis d’Avaray, whom Louis XVIII made a duke for having assisted him to enter a hackney-coach on the day when he emigrated

text: L'Aigle means 'the eagle', Napoleon's emblem, which Louis XVIII would not want to see on a petition. Spelt 'Lesgle', and explained as a contraction of the comic Lesgueules ('the gobs'), it becomes harmless, and the king laughs.
quote: This non-Bonaparte orthography touched the King and he began to smile.

text: Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), Bishop of Meaux, the grandest preacher of Louis XIV's reign, nicknamed 'the Eagle of Meaux'. Since Lesgle (l'Aigle, 'the eagle') signs himself 'de Meaux', his friends naturally call him Bossuet.
quote: As an abbreviation, his companions called him Bossuet.

text: French for persistent bad luck, a jinx. Bossuet greets misfortune by its nickname like an old friend: 'Good day, Guignon.'
quote: “Good day, Guignon,” he said to it.

text: A hundred francs, five gold louis, was a month's income for a modest clerk; spending it on one supper is 'unbridled extravagance' for a penniless student. Hence his joke calling his companion a 'five-louis jade'.
quote: “Pull off my boots, you five-louis jade.”

text: 'The Imaginary Invalid', Molière's last comedy (1673), about a hypochondriac who lives for doctors and purges. Joly, a medical student who checks his tongue in the mirror and lines his bed up with the earth's magnetism, is a junior version.
quote: Joly was the “malade imaginaire” junior.

text: A letter-puzzle: the capital letter R is a 'grand R', pronounced in French exactly like 'Grantaire'. He signs his name with it.
quote: he was in the habit of signing himself with this rebus: R

text: Real student haunts of the 1820s: the Café Lemblin at the Palais-Royal, a Bonapartist officers' café; the Café Voltaire near the Odéon; the Ermitage dance-garden on the Boulevard du Maine; and the barrier taverns of La Cunette and Le Combat. Grantaire's learning is a guide to where to eat, drink and dance.
quote: he knew that the best coffee was to be had at the Café Lemblin

text: Foot-fencing is savate, the French art of fighting with kicks as well as fists, popular among Paris workmen and students; singlestick (la canne) is fencing with a walking stick. Grantaire is a sceptic who can look after himself.
quote: boxing and foot-fencing and some dances; and he was a thorough singlestick player

text: Two famous acts of devotion in the Terror: Augustin Robespierre insisted on sharing his brother's arrest and death, and old Loizerolles answered to his son's name at the prison roll-call and was guillotined in his place. Grantaire sneers at both.
quote: Robespierre junior as well as Loizerolles

text: An old popular song in honour of Henry IV, the good king who loved wine and women; its tune carried many drinking songs, including Grantaire's 'J'aimons les filles et j'aimons le bon vin' ('We love the girls and we love good wine') in mock-peasant grammar. Under the Restoration it was practically a royalist anthem.
quote: “J’aimons les filles, et j’aimons le bon vin.” Air: Vive Henri IV.

term: Pollux, Patroclus, Nisus… Orestes and Pylades
text: The great pairs of devoted friends: Pollux and Castor, Patroclus and Achilles, Nisus and Euryalus (in the 'Aeneid'), Hephaestion and Alexander, and Orestes and his faithful Pylades. Eudamidas left his friends his debts in his will, and Pechméja was a minor writer devoted to his friend. Grantaire belongs among the men who exist as the second half of someone else.
quote: They are Pollux, Patrocles, Nisus, Eudamidas, Ephestion, Pechmeja.

text: A column carved as a standing woman holding up a roof, as on the Erechtheum in Athens. Bossuet propped against the café doorpost looks like one that has taken a day off.
quote: He had the air of a caryatid on a vacation

text: A light two-wheeled hired cab with a folding hood, the driver sitting beside the passenger. Cheaper and faster than the four-wheeled fiacre, it was the young man's cab of the 1820s (the English 'cab' comes from it).
quote: a two-wheeled vehicle proceeding through the place, at a foot pace and apparently in indecision

text: Paris law students paid fees for each term's inscription, and a professor could strike off a student who missed the roll three times, so the fees ('sixty francs in the gulf') were lost and the term did not count towards the degree. Answering for an absent friend was an old student trick.
quote: At the third call, unanswered, your name is erased from the list. Sixty francs in the gulf.

text: Nicolas Boileau (1636–1711), the satirist and lawgiver of French classical poetry, whose satires mock pedants. Bossuet credits him with the phrase to sharpen his portrait of the roll-calling Blondeau.
quote: who must be the malicious nose alluded to by Boileau

text: Latin from Psalm 2:10: 'Be instructed, ye that judge the earth'. The line was famous as the text of Bossuet's funeral orations, so this Bossuet uses it for his mock oration over the living Blondeau. Nasica (the 'big-nosed', a surname of the Scipios) and bos disciplinae ('ox of discipline') complete the parody.
quote: Erudimini qui judicatis terram

text: The lawyer's traditional boast was to 'defend the widow and the orphan'. Bossuet's twist (defending the widow, attacking the orphan) is a student joke about what lawyers actually do.
quote: I shall not defend the widow, and I shall not attack the orphan

text: A cab hired by the hour cost about a franc an hour, so living in one all year round would come to some nine thousand francs: the rent of a grand apartment. Bossuet congratulates Marius on his 'opulence'.
quote: You have there a rent of nine thousand francs per annum.

text: A cheap furnished lodging-house (hôtel garni) in the Latin Quarter near the old site of the Saint-Jacques gate, where students rented rooms by the month. In French 'hôtel' could mean any lodging house, as well as a private mansion.
quote: “Coachman,” said he, “hotel de la Porte-Saint-Jacques.”

term: 'The gray hue of a reassured rat'
text: A joke on the fanciful names of fashionable colours of the time ('mouse-grey', 'frightened-mouse', 'dying-monkey'). Courfeyrac means Marius's 'democrat-Bonapartist' is a timid in-between shade, neither one colour nor the other.
quote: “The gray hue of a reassured rat,” said Courfeyrac.

text: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century French verse tragedy on the ancient model (Racine, Voltaire), with its rules of unity and noble alexandrines, still staged in the 1820s. The Romantics, Hugo at their head, attacked it as 'bewigged'; Combeferre defends its right to exist as the duck exists beside the bird.
quote: “Down with tragedy dear to the bourgeois!” cried Bahorel.

text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau lived in the Rue Plâtrière (renamed after him in 1791) with Thérèse Levasseur, and admitted in his 'Confessions' that he left their five children at the Foundling Hospital. That the prophet of education and natural feeling did this was a favourite jibe of his enemies; Enjolras answers that he 'adopted the people'.
quote: Thérèse gave birth to them, Jean-Jacques represented them as foundlings.

text: What one called Napoleon was a political badge. Bonapartists said 'the Emperor'; republicans said 'Bonaparte', the general who had betrayed the Republic; royalists said 'Buonaparte', the Corsican. The Friends' refusal of the title surprises Marius.
quote: Not one of these young men articulated the word: The Emperor.

text: Latin, 'the beginning of wisdom', from Psalm 111: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom'. Hugo uses it for Marius's surprise: being shaken is where learning starts.
quote: Marius was vaguely surprised. Initium sapientiae.

text: An oil lamp with a hollow circular wick and a glass chimney, invented by Aimé Argand in the 1780s, which gave a far brighter, steadier light than candles. Lighting it 'solemnly' marks the start of the evening's meeting.
quote: The argand lamp was solemnly lighted.

text: The enormous wine cask in the cellar of Heidelberg castle, built in the eighteenth century to hold over 200,000 litres, a famous sight for travellers. Grantaire dreams of being one of the leeches applied to it.
quote: that the tun of Heidelberg has an attack of apoplexy

text: The refrain of the Book of Ecclesiastes ('Vanity of vanities, saith the Preacher; all is vanity'), traditionally ascribed to Solomon. Grantaire takes it as his text for a drunken sermon on the emptiness of everything.
quote: Ecclesiastes says: ‘All is vanity.’

text: The Roman emperor Caligula was said to have planned to make his horse Incitatus a consul. The English story that a king knighted a loin of beef, making it 'Sir Loin', is a popular folk etymology for 'sirloin', usually told of James I or Charles II. Grantaire's point: honours are toys.
quote: Caligula made a horse a consul; Charles II made a knight of a sirloin.

text: Antoine-Jean Gros was the painter of Napoleon's battles and ran the most popular studio in Paris in the 1820s. A rapin was a studio apprentice, the lowest of the art students, who ground colours and ran errands. Grantaire's pun links rapin and rapine, plunder: he stole apples.
quote: rapin is the masculine of rapine

text: Pliny the Elder records that Brutus, Caesar's assassin, doted on a statue of a boy by the Greek sculptor Strongylion, and that Nero took the same artist's Amazon 'Eucnemos' ('of the beautiful leg') on his travels. Grantaire uses it to show the noble republican and the monster emperor liking the same things.
quote: The Brutus who killed Caesar was in love with the statue of a little boy.

text: Pydna (168 BC) was the Roman victory that ended the kingdom of Macedon; Tolbiac (c. 496) the battle in which the Frankish king Clovis beat the Alemanni and, by tradition, vowed to become a Christian. Grantaire pairs them with Marengo and Austerlitz: history copies itself.
quote: The battle of Marengo copies the battle of Pydna

text: From Horace's 'Art of Poetry': words live or die 'if usage wills it', for usage is the judge and law of speech. Grantaire uses it to say that everything obeys success, even grammar.
quote: Si volet usus, says Horace.

text: Phocion was the upright Athenian general and statesman condemned to drink hemlock by his fellow citizens in 318 BC. Admiral Coligny, leader of the French Protestants, was murdered in Paris at the start of the Saint Bartholomew's Day Massacre in 1572. Both were killed by their own city.
quote: slew Phocion, as we might say Coligny

text: The cartoon figures of England and of the United States: John Bull the stout farmer, Brother Jonathan the lanky Yankee who preceded Uncle Sam. Grantaire rejects both: England for its 'Time is money', the America of 1828–1860 for its slavery and 'Cotton is king'.
quote: If I do not admire John Bull, shall I admire Brother Jonathan?

text: Grantaire's grim list of violent deaths in the Russian royal house: the Tsarevich Alexis, who died after torture on his father Peter the Great's orders (1718); Peter III, killed in 1762 after his wife Catherine took power; Paul I, strangled and beaten to death by officers in 1801. Hence the palace's 'flagrant insalubrity'.
quote: A decapitated Alexis, a poniarded Peter, a strangled Paul

text: The Dalai Lama of Tibet, a sacred ruler whose body and person were objects of veneration; Europeans told grotesque tales about it. Grantaire's retort is that Western courts made just as much ceremony over the queen's dirty shift and the dauphin's close-stool.
quote: what you find to laugh at in the Grand Lama

text: Paris slang for low drinking places: a bibine was a ragpickers' dive, a goguette a singing club in a tavern back room, a bastringue a cheap dance hall, a mastroquet a wine-seller, and caboulot and boui-boui both mean a dingy café. Grantaire rattles off the names like a connoisseur.
quote: the wineshops of the ragpickers are called ‘bibines;’

text: A student eating-house where a fixed-price dinner cost two francs a head, cheap but respectable. That is Grantaire's idea of the sybarite life, in the same breath as Persian carpets for Cleopatra.
quote: I eat at Richard’s at forty sous a head

text: The Greek father of medicine was said to have refused the Persian king Artaxerxes' rich gifts and an invitation to cure his army, rather than serve an enemy of Greece; the scene was a favourite of painters. Bossuet's restraining gesture reminds Grantaire of it.
quote: your gesture of Hippocrates refusing Artaxerxes’ bric-a-brac

text: In the nineteenth century 'spleen' meant a gloomy, bored melancholy, thought to be an English disease; the French borrowed the English word. Grantaire lists it with homesickness and hypochondria as his ailments.
quote: I have the spleen, complicated with melancholy

text: An emphyteusis is a very long lease, from the Roman law, by which a tenant held land for decades or forever on condition of improving it and paying a fixed rent. Bossuet's tangle of old Norman feudal law is meant to sound absurdly obscure.
quote: for all emphyteuses, leases, freeholds, contracts of domain, mortgages

text: A light comedy with songs set to popular tunes, the staple of the Paris boulevard theatres. Students and clerks often tried to write them for quick money; the stock names (Dorimon, Célestine, Colonel Sainval) show the formula.
quote: announced that a vaudeville was being sketched out

text: A mild French oath, 'heck!' or 'by Jove!', a softened form of a cruder word. The duel advice is in fencing jargon: attack, feints, parade (parry).
quote: bigre! and he is left-handed

term: A little Holy Alliance; Vaud and Gex
text: The Holy Alliance was the pact of Russia, Austria and Prussia after 1815 to defend thrones and religion. Bahorel's lovers' treaty has frontiers like the Congress of Vienna's: the Swiss canton of Vaud and the French Pays de Gex sit on either side of Lake Geneva, which became a treaty border. It is a joke about dividing a bed.
quote: On forming our little Holy Alliance we assigned ourselves each our frontier, which we never cross.

text: Staub was the fashionable Paris tailor of the 1820s and 30s, known for his trousers. Advising Joly to buy a pair there is advising him to dress like a dandy.
quote: Buy a good pair of trousers of double-milled cloth at Staub’s.

text: The Vignemale is a high peak of the Pyrenees, and Cybele the Phrygian mother-goddess, shown crowned with towers; Pan played pipes of reed; Io was the nymph turned into a heifer. The Pissevache is a waterfall in the Swiss Valais whose name means 'pissing cow'. Prouvaire's defence of the pagan gods ends in a schoolboy joke.
quote: I have always believed that Io had something to do with the cascade of Pissevache

text: A cheap edition of Louis XVIII's constitutional Charter of 1814, sold by the liberal publisher Touquet and bound with snuffboxes and handkerchiefs in the 1820s. To liberals the Charter was a guarantee; to republicans like Courfeyrac it was a gift the king could take back.
quote: On the table lay an unfortunate copy of the famous Touquet Charter.

text: The article of the Charter that let the king issue ordinances 'for the safety of the state'. It was the loophole a king could use to override the constitution, and Courfeyrac names it as the claw hidden in every royal grant.
quote: In all such grants there is an Article 14.

text: French for liveliness, go, high spirits that carry a group along. Hugo sets it against English 'humour' as two national kinds of wit, both on show in the room.
quote: that French thing which is called entrain

text: Courfeyrac's numerology: on 18 Brumaire of the Year VIII (9 November 1799) General Bonaparte overthrew the Directory in a coup and took power; on 18 June 1815 he lost at Waterloo and Louis XVIII came back. Brumaire was the 'month of mists' in the revolutionary calendar. Enjolras turns the pair into 'the crime and the expiation'.
quote: Place Louis in front and Brumaire behind, you have the whole destiny of the man

text: Latin, 'because I am called lion', from Phaedrus's fable of the lion's share: the lion claims the first portion of the spoil for no reason but his name. Enjolras means France needs no Napoleon to be great; it is great because it is France. (The text prints 'nomina'.)
quote: Quia nomina leo.

text: Marius's comparisons: the Emperor Justinian, who codified Roman law, as Napoleon did French law in the Civil Code of 1804; the mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace, a fellow member of the Academy of Sciences; and Merlin de Douai, the leading jurist of the Council of State. Napoleon was at home with lawyers and astronomers alike.
quote: he made codes like Justinian

text: The town on the river Niemen where in July 1807 Napoleon met Tsar Alexander I on a raft in midstream and dictated peace to Russia and Prussia: the high point of his power in Europe.
quote: at Tilsit he taught Emperors majesty

term: Cromwell blowing out one of two candles
text: An anecdote of Oliver Cromwell's thrift: he put out one of two candles burning on his table to save tallow. Marius cites Napoleon haggling over a curtain tassel in the same spirit: the master of Europe watched the small expenses too.
quote: like Cromwell blowing out one of two candles

text: Guns at the Hôtel des Invalides, the veterans' hospital in Paris, fired salutes for great events: births in the ruling family, and, under the Empire, the news of a victory. Parisians woke to the cannon and knew a battle had been won.
quote: to have the cannon of the Invalides to rouse you in the morning

text: Napoleon's great victories: Arcola (1796) in Italy, where he led the charge across a bridge himself; Marengo (1800) against Austria; Austerlitz (1805) over Austria and Russia; Jena (1806) over Prussia; Wagram (1809) over Austria again. Paris named bridges and streets after them.
quote: Marengo, Arcola, Austerlitz, Jéna, Wagram!

text: Combeferre's adaptation of the old song Alceste quotes in Molière's 'The Misanthrope' (1666): 'If the king had given me Paris, his great city, and I had to give up my sweetheart's love, I would say to King Henry: take back your Paris, I prefer my love.' Combeferre sings 'Caesar', 'glory and war' and 'my mother': freedom over glory. 'Ô gué' is a nonsense refrain.
quote: J’aime mieux ma mère, ô gué!

text: Citoyen, the form of address the Revolution imposed in place of 'Monsieur' in 1792, to make all men equal. Under the Restoration only a republican would use it, so Enjolras's 'Citizen' is a declaration in itself.
quote: “Citizen,” said Enjolras to him, “my mother is the Republic.”

text: The chapter title, from Juvenal's line that men rise with difficulty when 'res angusta domi', narrow means at home, hold them back. It means straitened circumstances: Marius's money runs out.
quote: The realities of life do not allow themselves to be forgotten.

text: The ordinary way a young man of good family without money raised cash: sell spare clothes to a second-hand dealer and the watch to a watchmaker. Twenty francs for a frock-coat and trousers, forty-five for a gold watch, against a hotel bill of seventy: Marius is left with ten francs.
quote: He paid twenty francs for the cast-off garments. They went to the watchmaker’s. He bought the watch for forty-five francs.

text: Courfeyrac's pun: in French langue means both 'tongue' and 'language'. Eating five francs while learning English means swallowing a language very fast, or a hundred sous (the same five francs) very slowly.
quote: That will be swallowing a tongue very fast, or a hundred sous very slowly.

text: The sixty pistoles M. Gillenormand ordered sent: six hundred francs in gold, which is also thirty louis of twenty francs each. It would keep a frugal student for half a year, and Marius sends it back with three francs in his pocket.
quote: Marius sent back the thirty louis to his aunt
